utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to greet everybody in the courtroom, the representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence teams, the accused. I would like to greet equally everybody present in the courtroom, and on may have of my colleagues, I would wish Mr. Petkovic a quick recovery. He's not with us today. We will proceed with our work. I'm going to render a decision with regards to the conference 65 ter. I will read slowly and I will check the transcript to so there are no errors in the interpretation. Yesterday the Chamber has received a joint motion by the Defence that request was submitted after the written motions pursuant to 92 bis regarding the municipality of Gornji Vakuf. The motion regards the Prosecution's request of 15 December 2006, the response by the Defence of 12 January, 2007, and the request to authorise a reply by the Prosecution dated 18 January 2007. In the motion that was filed, the Trial Chamber has exceptionally granted the motion. In the motion that was filed yesterday, the Defence asked us to hold a 65 ter Conference in order to deal with the following issues: Firstly, it seems that the Prosecutor agrees that the attacks on the villages in the municipality of Gornji Vakuf were targeted at legitimate targets. As a result of that, Defence will no longer have to present its evidence in that sense. Second, how does one interpret Article 92 bis, especially with regard to the period of time that is mentioned by the Prosecution? And three, does the Prosecution maintain that in Bosnia and Herzegovina there was no conflict between Croats and Muslims in 1991 and 1992? As regards point number one, in their request to authorise their reply, the Prosecution maintains that the fact that the villages in the municipality of Gornji Vakuf were defend -- defended or not is not relevant because the Prosecution has never maintained there was an illegal attack in the sense of the violation of the rules and laws of war and in keeping with Article 3 of the Statute. First of all, the Trial Chamber would like to emphasise that it is not its task to interpret the indictment as has been maintained by the Prosecution in their request. The question of the existence of a legitimate military target is particularly posed within the framework of destruction and killings that are invoked in paragraph 66 and 72 of the indictment. Also, this question is relevant in -- with regard to the allegations relative to the municipality of Gornji Vakuf. Therefore, the parties will both be requested to present evidence in that sense. As far as the question of the relevance of this point so as to allow for the cross-examination of one or several witnesses whose statements were filed pursuant to Article 92 bis of the Rules of this Tribunal, the Chamber would like to refer you to the decision that will be rendered in that regard. Second point, the application of Article 92 bis of the Rules and Regulations. The Chamber will present its position with regard to the application of the criteria which are provided for in Article 92 bis in its decision that it will render soon pursuant to the request filed in keeping with Rule 92 bis with regard to Gornji Vakuf. Item three: The fact that Muslims and Croats in Bosnia were engaged in joint defence at a certain point in time does not exclude the existence of a conflict. And finally, the Chamber does not deem necessary to deal with the aforementioned subjects contained in the motion by the Defence that has requested us to hold a conference in keeping with Rule 65 ter. In a nutshell, within the next few days the Trial Chamber is going to render a decision on the first point regarding Gornji Vakuf, and in that decision we will provide answers to all the questions that the Defence has filed in their submissions that we received yesterday. That would be it. And now, Mr. Bowen, again good afternoon to you. I hope you had a pleasant evening yesterday. I have to tell you immediately that your testimony will be finished today. Mr. Praljak has another 45 minutes, I believe. The registrar will confirm that. And without any further ado, I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Praljak, who is going to start asking you questions that he deems necessary and useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Bowen.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Before we start, I would kindly ask you once again to be as short as possible. I unfortunately don't have the time to discuss more questions with you, and I hope you will appreciate that 45 minutes is a very short time for everything that I would like to deal with. Therefore, I'm asking you to answer my questions whenever possible with a yes or no. And if I am need any additional explanations, then either I myself or the Trial Chamber will ask you to provide additional explanations. When you undertook your first trip from Sarajevo to Mostar, you passed through Konjic and Jablanica. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went on the outskirts of Konjic and I went to Jablanica, yes. Can I turn down the volume of my headphones? Is there a place that I can do that? Is it this? It's very loud. Okay. Yeah, that's better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that according to the 1981 census in Konjic there were 11.748 Croats and 22.826 Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Were you aware of the destiny of Croats from Konjic at the time when you passed through that area? What had happened to them from spring 1993 onwards? Were you aware of their lot?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that in Jablanica, according to the 1981 census, there were 2.630 Croats and 7.806 Muslims? Are you aware of that? Are you familiar with that information?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the lot of the Jablanica Croats from spring 1993 onwards?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can guess at what you're getting at in Konjic and Jablanica, but, no, I don't have precise details about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. On your right-hand side you have a rather big map on that table -- on that board on your right-hand side, and that map shows the positions of the BiH army in green, and in red it says the army of Republika Srpska, and in blue it says the Croatian Defence Council. And you will either confirm this or not: There is also the route that you took through the mountains from Jablanica to the entry into the Mostar valley, and this is depicted in a kind of red colour. And you will find all that on the right-hand side map which is the bigger of the two. Would that be approximately the route that you took from Jablanica across the mountains to get to Mostar? It should be marked in red. As far as you can remember, of course.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's -- it's -- what I'm looking at is in orange, but if it's that line then --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen it on a map before, but I'm assuming that's about right. It certainly starts in the right place and ends more or less in the right place.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the positions of the Republika Srpska army from the enclave, ebala [phoen], Konjic, and the positions of the HVO and the positions of the BiH army, are you familiar with all of these positions more or less?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to ask you this: When you finished the recording of your documentary, you took your Land Rover and went from Mostar to the north towards Jablanica again. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Which direction did you took when you left Mostar? Since we saw the spotlights, we saw that there was shooting, what route did you take from Mostar after the end of the shooting of your documentary? Where did you go to? Since the spotlights were on the north of Mostar, can I then say that you were northbound as you went towards Jablanica and further on north?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those spotlights weren't filmed on our departure. When we left, we left south towards Medjugorje, towards Medjugorje and then on to -- to Split. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would kindly ask you to look at document -- I -- the transcript that Witness Seid Smajkic authored here. He is a high Muslim official in Mostar. The page is 2991. I would like to call upon that transcript. The pages are 2991, 2992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We do not see the number of the document, of the transcript. If you could please repeat. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] The date is 4th of May, 2006. I apologise. The date is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any of that. I don't have that document. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: No, you don't have to have it, no. The date is 31st of May, 2006. The witness was Mr. Seid Smajkic, and the pages are 2991 and particularly 2992, 2993. The date is the 31st of May. I asked them him the following question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we don't have the document either. Maybe it has a number, but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for counsel. Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Sorry, this seems not to be working. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] It is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak is giving you reference of the page and date of the transcript of -- in this case. So he will read portion of the transcript. We are not -- we are necessarily not producing the transcript copies. I cannot help. I don't know whether it's working or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The question that I put to the witness, and I quote -- look at the map. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Can the map be put on the ELMO? It will be of assistance to the Trial Chamber and to the witness. And the map is the same one that I showed to the witness when I put this question to him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, my questions referred to the capacity of the road and the number of vehicles that could go on the road from Mostar towards Jablanica and Konjic. And particularly the Bijela Bridge and the bypass around Bijela Bridge. My question to the witness was this: "We can see that this is water, that this is a lake and an across that lake there is the Bijela Bridge which according to our information was destroyed by the Serbian artillery. Can you look at the Google satellite shot and can you see there is a road on the left and on the right? It was a dirt road that was built," and so on and so forth. Then His Honour Judge Trechsel asked whether it was 150 metres or 150 kilometres long, and then we established that this bypass was about 150 to 250 metres long. And I asked the witness whether I was right, and his answer was: "I know there was a bypass there and it was used by the BH army. This bypass was used by the BH army in order to establish contacts with Jablanica once the bridge had been blown up." And my next question to the witness was: "Correct. There was an asphalt road, Sarajevo-Konjic-Jablanica, and that road was interrupted. There was 150-meter long dirt road and then the asphalt road continues towards Blagaj, Mostar, and so on. Is that correct?" And the witness answered: "Yes, that is correct." Mr. Bowen, please, could you please look at the map, and could you show us where, in which place on the Jablanica-Mostar road the HVO interrupted that road in order to set up a check-up point? Where did the HVO put up a check-up point? Did you yourself see that the road was interrupted, or did you just rely on Mr. Humo's words on what he told you in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite follow you. Are you saying the road between Konjic and Jablanica, are you asking me if it was interrupted?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm talking about Jablanica-Mostar, sir. Could you please show on the map where was it that that road was interrupted by the HVO? My second question is: Did you ascertain that yourself? Did you go and see that with your own two eyes or did you just rely on Mr. Humo's words?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, perhaps earlier the previous appropriate question would be whether the witness has any knowledge of this whatsoever. Whether he's ever been on that road or knows anything about that road because there's no evidence that he's ever travelled on that road or knows anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bowen, the General seems to be asking you about the words of Commander Humo. He told you the road is blocked. You have to take an alternative route. And in his question, Mr. Praljak is indicating, it seems, that that road was never blocked. Did you rely on Mr. Humo's words, or did you go yourself to make sure that his words are right, that the road indeed was blocked and that you had to take an alternative route?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Neither of those two things, Your Honour. I relied first of all on the information that I had from the UN, from UNPROFOR, and from UNHCR in Sarajevo. I also relied on information I'd been given by the Spanish Battalion of UNPROFOR in Jablanica, and, no, I didn't drive down the road as far as I could see because during that war it was not my habit to drive towards the confrontation line just for the sake of it when the UN had already told me what the situation was on the ground. I think it would have been a pretty dangerous thing to do, to drive towards the BiH-HVO confrontation line just to see if I could talk my way through it. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Spanish Battalion at the time took that road to go from Jablanica to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They probably did, because UNPROFOR were able to go through confrontation lines in a way that journalists weren't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I will move on. Are you familiar with the German broadcaster CDF?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 1st of September, 1993 -- issued an order for a CDF team to be allowed to enter the Gabela collection centre and that the footage that they recorded at the time was aired across the world as one would say?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the name of your colleague journalist who was a witness before this Trial Chamber, Ed Vulliamy?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Ed Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that a witness before this Trial Chamber stated either on the 8th or 9th of September, 1993, allowed him to enter Gabela or Dretelj, I issued an order to that effect? Are you familiar with that fact?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can we now look at the document 300673. And while we are waiting for this to be done, are you familiar with the name of Sally Becker?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sally Becker was she the person in the press dubbed the angel of Mostar. Or maybe that was someone else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's the person. Does the name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's the same person that we're talking about, yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you please look at your screen. The Main Staff of the HVO, 1st of September, 1993, "approval whereby Ms. Sally Becker, the humanitarian aid worker, is allowed to cross the check-points and depart to the left side of Mostar controlled by Muslim forces ..." "On her way back Ms. Sally Becker will bring children ill and powerless persons with two sanitary vehicles." "All HVO soldiers are ordered to assist this humanitarian action by Ms. Becker ..." And this is signed by Major General Slobodan Praljak, myself. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could I ask, Mr. Bowen, did you know anything about this activity of Ms. Sally Becker in Mostar, this rescue action she was about to undertake, or have you learned it now only?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did know -- I'm pretty sure it was the same woman. There was a person called Sally who was dubbed, as I say, in the English press as the angel of Mostar. And I met her, in fact. I think it was my first trip in August, my first trip, and she was then talking about trying to do medical evacuation. I mean I should say as well that on our second trip there we entered from -- from the south, so we entered through the lines as well. It was only on my first trip that I walked in with the Bosnian army from the area near Jablanica of the on my second trip I came in and came out in a vehicle through the south side of the -- the south end of Mostar. Also on my first trip I left that way as well with -- with an UNHCR vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now can we have 3D 00696 brought up to the screen? 3D 00696. Mr. Bowen, you're going to see that this is a -- another document referring to Ms. Sally Becker, another approval, "whereby a free pass with a police escort on relation Citluk-Zitomislic-Vinjani Gornji is to be secured as well as the departure route to the Republic of Croatia." Sally Becker is here accompanied by seven other people who were either wounded or whatnot, again signed by the HVO commander, Slobodan Praljak. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: May I have the next document now, please, and it is 3D 00697. Once again dated the 15th of September, 1993, and it is permission to allow free passage with the police escort along the Citluk-Zitomislic-Mostar left bank route to Sally Becker and a sanitary vehicle of the HVO. And then we have two other names in an armed Land Rover and the signature there is Slobodan Praljak. Do you see that document?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Would you now take a look at another document. It is 3D 00693. 3D 00693. It is a book written by Sally Becker. "The Angel of Mostar" is the title. It's in English. And could we turn to page 74 of that book, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, while we're turning in the book could I just ask whether Mr. Praljak has any questions for this witness other than -- we're doing what we've done so many times before, simply putting documents in front of the witness and asking if Mr. Praljak reads them correctly. The witness has added no information or foundation to any of these documents in the last few minutes except it's the -- back to, Did I read that document correctly? Are we leading up to any particular questions for this witness or is this simply a reading test?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak. Would you go ahead and ask your question. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor -- well, Your Honour, the witness yesterday spoke about the impossibility of reaching the right bank and the obstacles put up by the HVO, which means me, what I did to prevent then arriving. Now, these documents and the other ones that I'm going to show the reverse side of the medal in my opinion, the reverse side of the coin. So it's all the period when the witness was there, and I consider it relevant to test the truth. May we now turn to page 74, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that may or may not be the case, but that don't change the fact whether this witness has any evidence to give about them or not. Mr. Praljak can present this evidence when he has the appropriate time and witness to do so, but to ask this witness to simply read a number of documents and say, "Have I read that correctly?", adds nothing to the record whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, Mr. Praljak has just explained to us that he wants to do. He has said that he's going to show a series of documents - that he's going to put them to the witness - that speak differently, and he wants to show that access was possible. That is how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I agree. I read this in the same time. But like the Prosecution, I believe that this is not cross-examination. This is presenting evidence. He's presenting documents as evidence to us, and it's not now that the Defence evidence is to be presented. There is a phase in the proceedings for the Defence to present their evidence, and as long as a witness doesn't have anything to contribute to the evidence, I think it is not correct to bring it before us in the context of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can assist on that for a moment. Once again, I'm sorry to have to return to this theme, Your Honour, but as long as we're hearing from the Bench that the Defence will have an opportunity to present witnesses at a later time, I have to keep, with respect, making the point that that contradicts the burden of proof on the Prosecution to present a prima facie case before the Defence is called upon to present evidence at all. The second point, Your Honour, is this: Mr. Scott objects to General Praljak showing the witness a document and saying, "Did I read this correctly?", and so on. About 80 per cent of the direct examination we've had from the Prosecution over the past three months has been exactly in that form, and we have been quite tolerant in not objecting to it, but I think if that's to be the practice, we should be given the same -- the same latitude. Your Honour, the real question here is that it seems to me based on the witness's answers today that the witness has now said that on the second trip he was able to enter Mostar without difficulty from the south side going through the lines, and that raises, I think, a legitimate question as to how that corresponds with the testimony he gave yesterday about the -- about the ease or difficulty of getting into West Mostar for the purpose of presenting a balanced presentation. So I think, Your Honour, I would invite you to give General Praljak some latitude in this cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, with all due respect, I did not talk about calling witnesses. I talked about presenting documents which have no relation to the witness and only remotely to what he says. And I did not say that all the work of Mr. Praljak was not correct. Certainly there are some absolutely useful questions, but this shooting of documents at the witness who cannot testify on them, because he does not testify with regard to these documents, that I continue to be of the opinion that it don't belong into this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if I -- I would -- as a common lawyer, I welcome that observation. I would simply ask that it be applied to the Prosecution also, because it has not been applied to the Prosecution so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may just adjust one quick remark, Your Honour. I think when documents are shown to the witness that might expose, for instance, a different set of facts than the witness has testified to, in other words, he wasn't aware of certain other facts that might -- that, had they been available to him at the time, might have -- he might have formed a different upon, I think in those instances such documents are relevant because it demonstrates the lack of information that the -- that the witness had at the time when he formed certain -- certain conclusions, and I think that's what General Praljak is trying to do. And lastly, I just want to say we don't know yet how much time will be allocated to the Defence. I haven't raised that issue at some -- because the matter is on appeal, but at some point we will need to tackle that issue, how much time does the Bench anticipate I giving the Defence so we can make some tactical decisions on what to present during this phase and perhaps what to present during our defence, if we so choose to put on a defence. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I asked the witness whether he heard -- he had heard of Sally Becker, and he said yes. He said he knew that she was referred to as the angel of Mostar in London, which is the title of the book by Ms. Sally Becker. Next, in the documentary we saw the state of children. Now, I would like to refer to an excerpt from Sally Becker's book to show what the HVO through Sally Becker sent out as a message to the left bank about the care of children and their mother -- and their mothers. I think that that is a valid question, and I beg the Court's indulgence to be able to ask it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before that is decided, Your Honour, the Prosecution must have a chance to respond to some of the things that have been said. It is indeed a recurring theme somehow that because the Defence does not necessarily have the burden at any time to put on a case, at the same time that we -- we cannot be constantly reasoning backwards from that saying they can tender any evidence at any time in the Prosecution case. One does not follow from the other. We have to meet our burden of proof, it's true, but you can't simply bring a witness into the courtroom and then bombard that witness with document after document that he or she knows nothing about and can add nothing about. I didn't object -- for the record and so it's clear, I did not object to the question whether the witness knew who Ms. Becker was because I thought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make my record, please? There's no translation. There's no translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give you the floor but I was a little taken aback by what you've just said. You said that you were surprised that the Defence was putting to the witness documents that he has no knowledge of. But, Mr. Scott, the Prosecution presents documents to witnesses all the time that witnesses have -- are not at all familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Not true at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you do the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Not true at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're trying to understand. There are certain witnesses that came into court. You showed them military documents and they knew nothing about those. They didn't know who the author of the document was except that there was a little point perhaps that the document referred to a situation they had lived through. Now the accused Mr. Praljak is putting a book to us titled "The Angel of Mostar," which has to do with what that lady experienced and so on and so forth. So I am trying to weigh up the two sides, the Prosecution and the Defence, and I don't see why you object to him presenting a book, whereas if we read the first paragraph on the first page, we can see as I did that there was a question raised about circulation and obstacles. So I think you should allow the Accused Mr. Praljak to ask his question. And that's where I don't understand you, Mr. Scott. But if you continue, perhaps I'll be able to understand you better.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have to respectfully disagree with the Court's -- with the President's observations. That is not what the Prosecution has done. When the Prosecution has called witnesses in connection with a document, the witnesses have talked about if not the -- not the source of the document, they have talked about the facts stated in the document. And to the best of your knowledge we may have erred on occasion, but to the best of our intention and practice the witness has always been able to add something to the document whether it was what was consistent what he or she experienced on the ground, "Yes, this in fact reflects what happened in our village around this time," et cetera, et cetera. So I don't agree whatsoever that this is the same thing. It is not the same thing. And that was my second point in response to Mr. Murphy. With all respect to my learned friend, that is not -- it was unfair to characterise the Prosecution case in the way that he has and we object to that. Thirdly, Your Honour, one of the points that was made by counsel suggested that Mr. Bowen's evidence this afternoon somehow is inconsistent tent with the evidence he gave evidence. I beg to differ. Of course, the transcript will speak for itself. I submit to the Court that Mr. Bowen's testimony how he got in and oust Mostar on each occasion is entirely consistent, entirely consistent with the way he testified about it yesterday and it's the record again will confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really don't wish to take up any more court time but I have to say one thing, and that is that I consider this entire discussion - we've lost seven or eight minutes as far as I was able to see - arose and came about with the intervention of my learned friend of the Prosecution, which was too early. It was premature. Mr. Praljak started with the document, and he wanted to get his question. So I think that the Prosecution jump the gun. And I think that was done intentionally to belittle the weight that the presentation would have. Secondly, the witness was there. The witness told us about what he saw and what he heard and what he knew. The Prosecution yesterday introduced the witness as a top expert for Bosnia. I don't want to go into the witness's expertise, but in Bosnia the message was clear. He knew everything about Bosnia, about Sarajevo, Mostar, and so on and so forth. So the object of the cross-examination is quite clear, and we must see what he does indeed know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, please proceed. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: On page 74 on Ms. Sally Becker's book, and you have it in English, of course, we see what Dr. Ivan Bagaric said, and he was the commander of the HVO military. He said: "We Croats have nothing against the innocent civilians in this war. We will give you permission to travel to eastern Mostar to evacuate not one but all the children from the hospital there and their mothers." Now, sir, my question is this: Do you know about the activities undertaken by Sally Becker and that all the children that she brought in were sent to Split for care and medical attention? Did you hear about that? Did you know about that? Are you familiar with that event?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that Sally Becker managed to evacuate a couple of children. I have to say, though, I stand 100 per cent behind what I said in the film about medical evacuation. And I also have to say that there was a very different approach to aid workers, especially freelance aid workers like Sally than there was to journalists from major news organisations. It's like comparing apples and oranges.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I apologise, sir, but I have to interrupt you. You told us that yesterday. There's no need to repeat it. May I have the next document please 3D 00700. Document 3D 00700. The document is the -- dated the 24th of September, 1993. Was Eamonn Matthews in your team? Brian Hulls, Nicholas Walker, and Vanessa Vasic Janekovic? Were they members of your own team?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my team. That was our document. That was when we entered Mostar from the south as I've said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It says approval that here with free passage is allowed to the BBC television crew to the final check-point of the HVO military police on Buna; the TV crew in the below cited composition makes a document -- is to make a documentary film in those areas." And then the names follow and it is signed by Slobodan Praljak, which is me. Is that how it reads?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is indeed how it reads in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I don't want to enter into polemics about what you said yesterday. Now, is it true that the HVO commander allows you to make this film on the left bank whereas he does not allow you to make a film on the right bank of the Neretva River? Does that seem to you be logical this kind of approval and lack of approval?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't seem logical, I agree, but that's what happened, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bowen, when I saw this document I asked myself the same question. I asked myself about logics. Listening to you yesterday, one gained the impression that there was a total block on the HVO side and that you were not able to make any documentary. Now we have a document here that seems to tell us the opposite, the contrary. Now, this document signed on the 24th of September, 1993, how did you obtain it? Tell us that, please. How did you obtain this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Eamonn Matthews obtained the document during his time in West Mostar. I think I've made clear throughout that we -- we entered -- when we -- on my second trip there we entered through the HVO lines coming from the south. I've been very consistent about that. And clearly it's impossible to pass through a confrontation line without the consent of the people who are involved in that confrontation. I -- as for the question of whether -- about the logic, you know, I agree. It's -- it does seem -- I'm a bit bemused. It is bemusing that, you know, one could get permission to film -- you know, cross through the lines but not get the permission we needed on General Praljak's side, but I'm sorry, that was the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But, Mr. Bowen -- may I ask one -- may I ask again the question which probably has been put to you before? Did you apply to film also on the western side of the Neretva?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said before -- I mean, I was not privy to the -- you know, the blow-by-blow discussions that Eamonn Matthews had when he visited with Vanessa Vasic Janekovic who was our translator. I wasn't privy to every bit of their discussion because I wasn't there and I only received a verbal report of it, but he same back and said we're not getting the cooperation we need to work on the west side but we have got permission to cross over into the east. Now, to -- to get that permission as well I'm pretty sure that he had the assistance of members of the EU Monitoring Mission, who I know assisted us in getting that particular piece of paper. That's certainly my recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I think that you have probably already answered my question, the one I wanted to ask you. I just wanted to check one thing. In the documentary that we were shown yesterday, there was certain sections that were filmed in West Mostar, west. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the film that we saw yesterday, are there any portions that were filmed in the HVO zone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As I said yesterday, there was nothing filmed in the HVO zone. The only sight you saw of the HVO zone was filmed from the forward positions of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, go ahead. The registrar tells me that you've already used up 40 minutes. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm surprised to learn that as well. Could you check that, Mr. Registrar? It seems a little surprising. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I haven't used up more than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The registrar has just informed me -- well, he apologises because it's yesterday and today, 30 minutes in all. 32 minutes. Go ahead anyway. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did Mr. Matthews inform you, Mr. Bowen, that I asked him and entreated him, implored him to come to the right bank as well and to film both sides, which is a minimum of journalist ethics that would require him to do so? Did he inform you about that?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's logical -- would you agree with me when I say that it would be logical to have allowed you to go to the left bank and to order the snipers and artillery and me -- expulsion of people, me to allow you to film that?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't get the whole translation of that. Could you repeat it, please? I can't see the transcript in front of me either, so ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is it a logical conclusion that I allowed the BBC crew to go to the left bank and then proceeded to order snipers to shoot, to order the artillery to fire, people to expulse the Muslims so that this could provide good subject matter for a war film and a documentary? Do you think that's absurd?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's a matter of whether it's absurd or not. We filmed what we saw on the east side of Mostar. We didn't fabricate that. Those are things that happened. You know, I cannot comment directly on what you told Mr. Matthews because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. The next document, 3D 00733. 3D 00733 is the number of the next document that I'd like to show on e-court. It is the book by Sefer Halilovic on strategy. Do you know who Sefer Halilovic is?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It is entitled, "A Sly Strategy." On page 138, I'm not sure what page it is in the English version. It might be the same page number, number 138. It says that the necessary documentation for an operation entitled Neretva '93, Delic with his stamp and seal allowed has given permission for everything to go forward and we are going out in the field, et cetera. Now, in that same book, "A Cunning Strategy," according to Sefer Halilovic the BH army should have been brought to the western borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you know that Neretva '93, that operation, according to the words of Sefer Halilovic, we can't see them on our screens, unfortunately, should have reached the western borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina? That's what it was designed to do. Do you know about that, Mr. Bowen?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not familiar with these -- these orders. I certainly wasn't familiar with them at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know the time of the operation, how long it lasted, when it started and when it finished? It's duration. But if you didn't hear of the operation itself, then I'm sure you can't tell it us about the duration either.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can we agree on this point, that the western borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina are the borders towards Croatia, that is to say from Dalmatia stretching to the south, Dubrovnik, Split, and further on, are those the western borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I guess so. I'm familiar with the map, yes. The west, yeah. There's [Microphone not activated] of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. As you from the 24th of September were in Mostar yourself -- I'd like document 3D 00740 to be shown now, please. 3D 00740 is the number of the document. It is a combat order by the command of the 4th Corps signed by the 4th Corps commander, Mr. Arif Pasalic. You met Mr. Arif Pasalic, and you know that he was the commander of the 4th Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I met Pasalic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on page 1 -- we don't have time to go through all the documents, but they will be tendered later on with the maps. It says: "In-depth the Operative Group south and infiltrated groups inflicted heavy losses --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, the document that you mentioned we don't seem to have in our binders, 740. The last document was signed by Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it should be the first document after the list, because it was subsequently added. So not going by the numbers but immediately after the list. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, you see the document. You say you know Mr. Pasalic, and we'll check out his signature later on. In point 1, Mr. Pasalic says, "the enemy, the Ustasha forces of the HVO," so he's already calling us Ustasha forces. And then in point 2, he says the forces inflicted heavy losses on the enemy in live force and military materiel. And then he goes on to say the North 2 Operative Group forces with the BiH group engaged in active operations at Djubrani and Planinica and the Mostar valley. May we have the last page on our screens now, please, the last page. And the signature is that of Mr. Arif Pasalic. But let's look at point 7. It says: "Attack readiness only when the signal zapad," or west, "is given. Combat readiness with the zapad signal." The next document is 3D 00736.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say that actually in the English version; it says "Illegible."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: This is a handwritten document, and I don't know why it hasn't been translated. It is not illegible. It says: "The activities to be carried out only when the west signal is given," but we will leave it to the translators to correct their work. Now can I have 3D 00736 brought up on the screen? This is an order for attack. The date is 15 September 1993. It is approved by Commander Arif Pasalic, and this was a very long order which was signed by Commander Samir Drljevic. He is commanding an axis of the attack. Obviously we cannot read the whole order, but does it say that this is an order for attack which analyses all the axis that the BiH army is supposed to attack? And can I have the last page now, please, where it says how many combat sets should be ready and distributed to every man and every unit. And it was sent to the 1st Battalion, the 2nd Battalion, the 3rd Battalion, the 4th Corps Command. It was signed by Commander Samir Drljevic. There is also a BiH army stamp. Do you see the stamp, Mr. Bowen? Can you see it? No, you can't see it. Okay. Very well then. You don't have it in your version. Did you ever hear --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the English version; it's not stamped. I see the stamp now, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question to you is this: Do you know anything about these activities of the BH army and the preparations for these activities at the time? However, this question will be better illustrated by the following document that I'm going to show to Mr. Bowen. Unfortunately, because of the -- Mr. Bowen, I'm going to read to you some things from Esad Sejtanic book. Have you ever heard of Esad Sejtanic in Mostar? Have you ever heard of that name? Does it ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe a small bell. Not a big one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Sejtanic authored the book about Herzegovinians, "At the Fiery Doors of Bosnia." This was a publication that was published. I'm going to read it slowly and ask you what you knew about the activities described in the book at the time when you were on the ground. On page 180 it says this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Is this a document we should also have? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: No. No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 180 it says: "The line of defence were established against the Serb forces but they were not active in combat sense. However, on the same lines there was smuggling of all sorts of goods, and for the most part with the bare necessities that were lacking such as flour and sugar," and so on and so forth. On page 181 it says this: "Within the framework of the preparations for the planned operative -- combat operations there was an open talk about the possibility that the Serbian side would help us by direct artillery support and by delivering to us critical materiel and equipment, and primarily by the sale of a large number of artillery shells of various calibre." Later on I'm going to ask you about how familiar you were with the artillery of the 4th Corps, but let me continue. "I attended a meeting on the contact line with the Serb forces in the village called Busak where Safet Orucevic, Fatima Leho, and Sefkija Dziho defined the conditions under which the Serb side would help us in our combat activities. The Serb side agreed to all the conditions. They would give us a -- one 128-millimetre howitzer with the team and 200 projectiles, and so on and so forth. As a token of our gratitude for the cooperation so far, Safet Orucevic gave Novica Gusic, the commander of the Nevesinje brigade, almost a brand new GX Golf."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. So far I have refrained from asking questions or in a way calling into question about the major themes which you are following and also the -- yesterday afternoon other colleagues of yours have followed by the Defence team. Somehow I fear that I didn't want to interrupt you when you asked the witness, Mr. Bowen, about why he did not go to West Mostar. For me, the question is what he has presented to us is about East Mostar, Mostar east. So now somehow I fear that the Defence, you, and others will address this issue: What happened in East Mostar? And it is not for me at least, not the major issue why he did not go to West Mostar. It is my first problem which I would really like to have an answer. Now, the second question is now you have now mentioned various interviews and parts of a book, and you have been speaking about the intentions and the discussions with the Serbs, et cetera. Again, I am a bit surprised because it has nothing to do what the witness, Mr. Bowen, has told us yesterday about the situation in East Mostar. So I real little feel that a cross-examination should concentrate on the major problem which most exposed or which had to be exposed by a given witness. It is not about only Mr. Bowen but all the witnesses which we so far have listened to, and that is why I really feel that the Defence have to address this question: What happened in East Mostar? What was true or what was false in that documentary which we have seen yesterday? For me it is the major importance, and I would like to -- to ask you and also the other colleagues to address these points which I raised. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak -- I will give you the floor, Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Praljak, I ascribe to the words of my colleague. This witness has come to talk -- to it talk about what was going on in the West Mostar, and to that intent the Prosecution has shown us a video which spoke about various subjects, and as my colleague has just said, and he has right, we Judges are not interested what was going on there. If you want to ask him questions about Mostar, West Mostar, that's okay. Now you're asking him about Serbs and contact lines, which is interesting, but the witness is here, and we would like to hear what is important and what is relevant in terms of the indictment, which has a probative value. The questions that you're asking that might be interesting from the general point of view do not go in the heart of the matter that we, the Judges, have to deal with. That's why my colleague has told you, you are wasting your time, Mr. Praljak, for nothing. Do you understand that? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas has asked the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be of some assistance, Your Honour, and I think this is what -- the dilemma that the Defence faces in general, aside from the time limitations. The video begins with the gentleman talking about Croatian propaganda echoing over the front line, and he goes on about the aiding and abetting of the Croatian government and there was some questions posed yesterday. Now, I dare say that the gentleman comes in to the theatre over there, that part of the war, sort of in the middle of the third act, or the third scene of a four-act play. He doesn't know what's happening before. He certainly doesn't know what's happening during and/or afterwards. He sees one side. And yet he is projecting the entire film from the east side point of view. He claims that he can't go on the west, yet he gets permission from the west to travel to the east. That's a different story. But nonetheless, I think if we're going to paint a correct picture and to see what, if anything, we're going to give -- how much value we're going to give to the film, granted I think that we do see some sniping. We do see the conditions in the hospital. That is undeniable. It's on the film. But on the other hand -- on the other hand -- on the other hand, the gentleman comes in without having done his homework and certainly doesn't know what's happening in the general theatre. And I think what General Praljak is trying to do is paint the picture that -- that what we don't see in the video is the army of BiH's orders for the attack. He doesn't know what's happening beforehand. He's being led by somebody to see certain things, and it's a one-sided, lopsided view. Now, if the video is coming in solely for the purpose of showing what the conditions were in the -- the hospital conditions were on the east side, that's one thing this, but that's not the reason they're bringing it in. They are they're bringing it in to show that the east side is under siege. Very well. Don't you think it might be relevant for the gentleman to know what is happening on the west side and why the West is perhaps attacking? Who's attacking whom? And I think that's being what is brought out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You don't think that's right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No. We will get a full picture by many witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're trying to help you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You cannot expect one witness to draw an entire and even to draw a very equitable picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This is -- what -- what the purpose is with the presentation of this documentary is not so important. We will place it in its place within the entire thing, and you can be assured that we can very well see that this is to a certain extent one-sided. We will also hear the other side. But we cannot get a full picture in the context of this one testimony. It's just asking too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree. I agree. And with that, Your Honour, my comfort level is, you know, slightly better. Not much, but slightly. But thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave. Just four sentences, literally. And I would like to use them to show you that the questions by General Praljak are in direct connection with the documentary and with the words of our -- today's witness, journalist Bowen. In the first minutes we saw the following sentences being uttered by Mr. Bowen. "General Pasalic was not happy, although he should have been. During the 30 hours of intensive -- intense fighting, his men managed to break through a neighbourhood which was under the Croat control and up to the hill called Hum, which towers above Mostar. This is probably one of their most important single victories in this war." It seems that the witness knew the BH army was engaged in offensive activities. In the 37th minute of the film it says, "However, from Sarajevo an order came that they had to withdraw." In other words, the witness knew that there had been an order that came from Sarajevo and, with your leave, just two more sentences about the ammo supply, which is also decided on by Sarajevo. The next sentence says: "In any case, independent Muslim commanders also buy weapons from the Serbs." Which means that it was the Witness Bowen who introduced the Serbs into this rather than Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bowen, you have listened to interventions by one and the others. Mr. Praljak maybe will not receive this well; however, Ms. Alaburic has clarified the situation to a certain extent. Tell us, when you were there, when you were filming in August and September, did you personally witness some military operation by the BiH army against the HVO? Because you see, what we see in the documentary that you authored, we see civilians that are crossing over through those areas. We see the BiH army soldiers. We see civilians crossing the river Neretva during the night. We also see dead and wounded people in the hospital. This is what is depicted in your documentary. However, there is nothing about any attacks against the HVO. The Defence puts it to you that there were attacks during that period of time. However, you were there and we will have other witnesses who will come and testify so this issue will be clarified even further, but now that you are here can you tell us whether you can tell us, "Yes, while I was filming there were attacks by the BiH army," or, "While I was filming there was nothing going on, on the BiH army side. The situation was calm and peaceful"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were there for the filming of the documentary, General Pasalic was able to spend a lot of time with us. The -- the operation, which I think those orders that we saw referred to, was by the time we got there in late September I think over with. As the lawyer there said, he described how his forces had made some progress towards the mountain of Hum and then had withdrawn. He said it was because of orders from the capital in Sarajevo. Now, I was interested to see those documents because it sort of bears out what we were saying in the film, that there had been a pretty serious military operation going on there which, by the time we got there, was over. I was also interested to get confirmation about what the BiH people told me about receiving weapons from the Serb side. I just want to say in case there's any misapprehension about the documentary, this was never at the time presented by the BBC than a report from one side. Front line, and I made clear throughout that my -- my interpretation of what was happening there was that the Bosnian army was fighting a war, fighting hard, and fighting successfully. At no point have I tried to suggest that they were lambs who were just waiting to be slaughtered. They were fighting very hard. And I've been to many wars and I know when one side is fighting hard and the other side is fighting hard, people get killed on both sides. I mean, that is war. That is the way it is. I think that the documents that we have been seeing, I just wish I had access to them at the time, because they bear out what my reporting actually discovered on the scene through talking to people. To -- sorry, Your Honour. I'll directly finish answering your question. While we were there, there were exchanges going on across the confrontation lines, and there was artillery as well and there was sniping. But as far as I could see there was no concerted military operation. The commanders were pretty relaxed. For example, there's a scene in the film where the commanders get together in a house and they have some drinks and afterwards, we didn't show it, but they were having target practice on a wall. They were very relaxed. So I think that suggests that this military operation that's been referred to was over with by the time that we were filming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the 15 days in September while you were there, were there at any given time BiH offensives against the HVO, or was there just a -- a separation line and things were just as usual, shots across the separation line? What did you experience on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My memory of it is that there was -- there was pretty constant shell-fire and small-arms fire but nothing -- there was no military offensive as such going on. They weren't at the time we were there trying to break out of the line, for example. Why can I say that? As I say, I deduced that from the state of mind of the commanders, the fact that the movements of troops around the town. We moved to the north and the south of the whole enclave, and as I say, the commanders were relaxed. The men were certainly going up to do their duties on the front line, but normally during an offensive you would expect soldiers could be moving in the rear echelon. You'd expect to see casualties coming back, you know, in fair numbers. And you'd expect to see pretty constant and quite intense shell-fire. I've been in different wars and quite a few offensives, and I've seen that. And at the time I would say that the level of activity that we saw was more along the lines of -- while we were filming there, was more along the lines of to'ing and fro'ing, fighting back and forth across the confrontation line, no specific offensive as such. However, I knew that there had been that intense fighting because I'd been fold about it and between my first visit and my second visit I'd seen more damage on the east side. There was a lot more by September than there had been in August. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I simply want to challenge the credibility of this witness, to put it simply.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: From the book, on page 183, it says this: "Combat activity started in the early morning hours on the 20th of September." Again we're talking about the year 1993. "And they followed a plan, especially on the flanks where we expected to achieve successes that would then be used to prolong the activities against the city centre it. I'm asking the units --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges are listening to with a lot of attention because are trying to challenge the credibility of this witness, and you're reading from a book, from page 183, but we don't have the book. It would be in your best interest, if you believe that this is a key document, that you should have this document translated and that you should provide it to us. Don't get me wrong. I trust you when you're reading the document, but it would be much better if we had the book ourselves. You have read the sentence out. Can you now ask the witness questions. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, last night we did not manage to have the book translated. Together with the -- a nurse [as interpreted] and the orders that arise from the book will be submitted to the Trial Chamber. Will you allow me to read two more sentences it says the action in the city centre had some successes in the Balinovac neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is the Balinovac neighbourhood part of Mostar on its western side? Do you know that Mr. Bowen?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Balinovac neighbourhood. On the west side. I'll take your word for that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And now can you pay attention to the rest of this sentence: "With a strong, and I repeat very strong Serb artillery, the success was quite likely." And this is on page 180. It says there towards "the sequela of the combat activities on the units of the 4th Corps were really terrible. During the retreat to our starting positions we had over 30 dead and about a hundred slightly and seriously wounded." Mr. Bowen, this started on the 20th and lasted until the 30th when everything was called off, according to the words that we heard in your documentary. Did you know anything about this? And if you didn't know anything about such major offensive operations, how come you didn't know a thing about such major offensive operations? This is my question to you.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect the end of the operation was a bit less major than he was suggesting because I was there at the time, and while as I say there was a lot of -- there was activity going on the whole time, no one said to me, "We've got a major offensive going." General Pasalic was able to spend the whole of one evening with me and then the whole of the following day in a very relaxed mood. If a major offensive had been going on then he hid it very well. He said that by the time that we got there and we started talking about this that the fighting was over with. That level -- that offensive, anyway, that operation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Can the witness now be shown this piece of paper? For my next question, can the piece of paper be put on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yesterday in your documentary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, while you're putting your questions we are looking at the map, and the Judges have just established that Balinovac is in Mostar west. So not in the eastern part of Mostar but at the extremity of the town, in the western part of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not a -- I was there during the war for a period of time, and I was not able to get to know every district of Mostar and every place name. So I will accept what you're saying about that, but I wasn't familiar with that -- or if I was, I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There is no inconsistency. The transcript says that the Balinovac neighbourhood was on the west side on page 38, line 12. Lines 8 to 12. So I'm not sure what the inconsistency is. That's what's been said all along. It was on the west side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no lack of consistency. I just wanted to make it clear for the record that Balinovac is in western Mostar rather than in eastern Mostar. We have to know that. You, Mr. Scott, should know that there could be an attack that came not from the western part of Mostar but from somewhere else. That's why it is necessary to establish where Balinovac is on the map of Mostar. Let's move only. The time runs quickly. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I believe that I have some more time, because the lawyers and yourself have used up a lot of my time. Could you please look at the document. Yesterday in your document we saw a dead woman's body on the bank of the Neretva. Since the Judges visited Mostar and they saw that Neretva runs through a very deep canyon in Mostar, and judging by the bridges that connect the two banks of the river, the banks are some 15 or 20 metres long -- high, and very steep. I tried to do some mental arithmetics and at the height of the bank of 20 metres and at the place where the Neretva is some 50 metres wide, that's one scenario. And the other scenario is if the Neretva is 60 metres wide and the banks are 20 metres high. And if the HVO positions were some 350 metres away from the Neretva River, I tried to calculate how high should a sniper or a rifle have been in order to hit a woman washing clothes on the river Neretva at this angle. My question to you, Mr. Bowen is this: When you saw the dead woman's body on the bank of the Neretva River, Mr. Bowen, did you go down and did you look at the opposite side? Because you said the woman had been sit from the HVO side. Did you look at the angle at which the woman could have been hit? And as you were looking, did you see a building that should have been some 200 or 100 metres high according to my mental arithmetics, which I think is good. So my question is, did you go down? Did you look at the opposite side, the opposite bank? And did you establish where the sniper could have been shooting from in order to kill that woman? Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I understand your question, and for your information I can tell you that that picture was filmed by our cameraman Nigel Chandler and I wasn't with him because I was with the other cameraman when he was working. So I wasn't with him when he was filming so, no, I was not able to make those checks.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But, Mr. Bowen, you make the conclusion in your film, and I can't hear the words of your cameraman, I can hear your own words, where you say that the woman that your cameraman filmed at a distance of 10 metres was killed by a sniper from the HVO side. Is that some poetic -- that extreme poetic licence which should not be allowed? Could you answer that question, please?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it's not poetic licence it was based on what the -- the witnesses to it and the people who were there were saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, if we look at the map of Mostar, do you have an idea as to where this woman was washing? Was it on -- on the upper side north of Carinski Most, or was it near Cernica or Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't got a map at happened actually. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: On that other map to your left, Mr. Bowen. You have that map. To your left.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got a very clear one here too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's a good map there.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say. I don't want to get this particular thing wrong. So I think if I was going to answer that directly I would be making a bit of a guess because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Don't then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- because I didn't have the benefit of this map at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Don't if you can't say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't really want to guess. I've got some idea, but it would be 50 per cent guesswork and, you know, calculation and -- plus based on where I think we were at any given time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] May I have another document; it is 2D 0086, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you've almost used all of your 45 minutes, so this has to be the last document that you're presenting. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] 2D 00086 is the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Federal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen, yesterday you said in your film, in your documentary, that you were able to conclude on the basis of some factors that the Croatian army was in Mostar -- in the Mostar area and that was pursuant to orders from Zagreb, on the basis of some ID cards or whatever. Now, according to this document compiled by the security sector of the HVO, it lists 14 British citizens. Are you familiar with any of the names on that list? First of all, did you know that those people were in Mostar? Did you know that they were in the BH army units? And do you know, looking at the other pages of the document, that they were paid in Croatian dinars by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recognise those names. I didn't know that there were British mercenaries on the BiH side at that time. I wish that I had, because I would definitely have tried to contact them and interview them, because it would have been an interesting development and a strong story.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And what about your friends Mr. Humo and Arif Pasalic? How come they didn't introduce you to your compatriots? That's one question. And second, did somebody from the British government send them? Do you have any information about that? And the fact that a group of Englishmen are on one side, can we conclude that they were sent by the British government or the Queen or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I only wish Humo and Pasalic would have introduced us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. This is a hypothetical on the part of Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Does --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or, rather, a hypothesis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. The -- I would have -- would the British government have sent them? I know they had special forces soldiers moving around quite large areas of Bosnia, but I certainly saw nobody who looked like a British soldier while I was in Mostar, and I don't believe that the British government were intervening militarily on the side of the BiH government in Sarajevo. If that's true, it would be a very interesting development even now, and if I had more documentation, I promise you we'd do a documentary about it. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry my time is up. I could go on asking a lot of questions about the artillery, the artillery by the hospital, the military facilities in Mostar of the BH army within the urban centre, the number of Croats on the eastern bank, the number of Muslims on the west bank, and the difference between ethnic cleansing and persecution and everything else that the witness presented here. And I think that the witness was too hasty in making his conclusions on many of these points, but I'm sorry, I have no more time. Thank you, Mr. Bowen for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we end, Mr. Praljak, you said what you said, and I'd like as the Judge to tell you that I don't have the right to questioning you, but I'm telling you that you said this on page 25, line 2, and you repeated it on page 24, line 21. You said, in order to allow the witness to make his report, that you gave an order to the artillery and sniper to cease-fire. You said that on two occasions. It's in the transcript. You can check that out. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] No, completely wrong. My sentence was a very clear one as a hypothesis, and the question was this: Is it logical that a commander of an army issues the BBC with a permit or gives permission to go to the opposite enemy side to make a documentary then, once having granted them that permission, permission to do so, to issue an order? This is a hypothetical. To issue an order to their snipers and artillery and people who are expelling the Muslims, persecuting the Muslims, for him to be able to film a document which will be later awarded, given an award. So that was something absurd that I was stating and I wanted to hear from Mr. Bowen whether he agrees with me, or whether crimes of that kind is quite a normal thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that explanation. Any re-examination, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, about two questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Mr. Kovacic would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have a very brief question. I need two minutes. Mr. Praljak didn't have time to do so, and I consider it to be important before Mr. Scott continues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bowen, I am Defence counsel for Mr. Praljak. In the documentary that you showed us yesterday, it is at 8 minutes 49 seconds, at one point you made a comment and you said, "Up until now -- so far, except for the tannoys relaying Croat propaganda, not all that different," et cetera, et cetera, you clearly imply that there is a difference in how Croatian propaganda is being disseminated, the tannoys. Do you know what I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm looking at the transcript now. I mean what --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At 8.49. 8 minutes, 49 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at it, sir. If I can explain what my line was referring to. I said that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: May I interrupt you? All I wanted to observe was that you know what I'm referring to and I'll ask my question now. I'll go --

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. Sure, absolutely. Sorry, yes, I understand. I do know what you're referring to and I'm reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So along with that comment the audiotape in the background you can hear a female voice from this loudspeaker or the tannoys that you're talking about, and we listened to it carefully, and the woman says the following words: "The signal for the -- the code for Republic of Croatia is 385. For Slovenia it is," et cetera, et cetera. My question to you is this: Do you speak Croatian?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't but I know what they were staying on that particular part of the -- I can speak a bit of it to -- I understand -- I knew it was numbers when we went through the tape. The point is, though, if I can explain, that broadcast went on for many hours a day and we listened to it a lot and I listened to it with our translator who described to me what was being said. It so happened that in the edit the piece that they picked up because it was a clear piece of audio, was that. That doesn't take anything away from the reason that the tannoys were -- the HVO did not set up those tannoys to give people information about direct dial services in a city with no telephones. You know, they were there for a purpose, and that purpose was to try to get over the political propaganda points of one side. And if you were at the front line areas and I would have spent time with people who lived in apartments there, they heard it the whole time, often at night as well.
