And we heard it and as I say I sat there with a translator and she translated it for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So your interpretation of those words that we heard in the background over the tannoys was part of the propaganda. Now, please explain this to me: What's that got to do -- what's that propaganda got to do -- or why should the Republic of Slovenia be mentioned and the area code for Slovenia? Is Slovenia involved in that propaganda as well? Because your answer -- by your answer you make your conclusion, but I'm asking you about the words that can be clearly heard there in the background. Among other things, we heard the area code given for the Republic of Slovenia. Is that then Slovenian propaganda? Can I interpret it that way? I would be able to following the same logic that you're saying that it's Croatian propaganda. If you apply the same logic, that's how that can be interpreted. So can you explain that to us please?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think what you've said is an absurd statement. I've made it clear that for many hours a day the views of the Croatian side were being broadcast over the front line on tannoys. Now, perhaps they were replaying something that for some reason had a public information element regarding the best numbers to call, but as I say there were no telephones in the city anyway and that broadcast was not about the best way to make telephone calls. Frankly, we didn't make a big deal of it. We -- I had to explain why there was tannoy noise on the tape, and I said that it was not all that different from any other urban front line in Bosnia-Herzegovina because that was certainly the first time that I'd come across a tannoy broadcasting for many hours a day over a front line. I mean, that was the point I was making.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, did you record some other portions of that as you say, propaganda or just what we heard? The question is simple. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, without having the rest [phoen] of the tapes here, I can't answer yes or no. I was with the translator having it translated to me. You don't -- when you're making a television documentary, you just film bits of things, and I imagine what happened -- the normal professional technique, Mr. Praljak will tell you about this, is that as well as doing the pictures, which is -- it's an on-off with the video, so you get a broken up soundtrack, what happens then is the cameraman records a section of sound that you put over the edited version. And our cameraman who don't speak Croatian clearly decided to record the section where they gave dialling tone information, direct dial information. However, in my notebook there was the other stuff that the translator gave to me which was a description of what the broadcaster was actually saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you for the explanation of technology, but I'm sure you will agree that on the documentary we saw there was no other propaganda, as you call it, except for those five or six words that I quoted. Is that correct? Yes or no? Is there or isn't there?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recorded what was happening there. It so happens and this was probably as well because, you know, they should have chose -- listen, I accept they should have chosen a better piece of sound for that section of the picture, because it is a bit confusing. I accept that. But I'm telling you there was propaganda coming out of those tannoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. To round up and conclude, this was your selection of an excerpt of that propaganda. Would that be right then?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Us collectively. I wasn't involved in selecting that little piece of signed, no. But I'm telling you, as I said -- excuse me. I made my point already about the fact it was happening. I mean, I don't make things up. I do -- I want to say this because there have been all kinds of, Your Honour, allegations being made about my journalistic -- my professionalism. I've been a journalist for a long time and I'm telling you I've discovered and I know and I've been trained that you don't make things up. There was no need to make things up in East Mostar. What was happening there was extraordinarily dramatic. That's the reason why we're still walking about it 14 years later. It was very dramatic and it was all there. It was all laid out in front us. I did not make that up. And what's more, I stand a hundred per cent behind what it was I reported there. I had no stake in telling lies about the war, I can assure you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Bowen --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But Mr. Bowen, my -- what I was implying is very clear. You're talking about propaganda, and on the documentary that you played regardless of the technological explanation you gave, that you said that others did that and so on, you said that there was Croatian propaganda there. Now, if you listen to it and many others who understand Croatian, if they were to understand it, they hear a message that has nothing to do with propaganda whatsoever. So that's the only thing I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That point -- the point, I think, has been very clearly made. I have a -- I have two questions, actually, to Mr. Bowen. The first is: Were you aware of what this passage actually meant? Had that been translated to you before or had you just trusted your cameraman that he would take a representative sample?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know what "tri, osam, pet" means, and "tri, osam, and devet," and so on. I know what that means. I -- it meet help if I very briefly in two lines explain how we would work in that situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Couldn't you just answer the question? Were you aware that someone who understands Croatian hears these telephone informations in the documentary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When we were viewing the tape, when we were viewing the finished product, before it was broadcast with other translator who was with us in -- in Mostar, she made the same point, that it was -- it was just numbers, and it was as she explained. So yes, we were well aware of that. But for technical reasons, unfortunately, that was the clearest piece of audio we had. It doesn't get away from the fact, and as I say I would stake my journalistic reputation on it, that was -- propaganda was what was being broadcast. They didn't set up tannoys to just give people the football commentaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's my second question, Mr. Bowen, Can you give an example? Do you recollect --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- a sentence that was actually spoken and leads you to say it was propaganda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact sentence as an exact word-for-word quote, but the sense of -- when I was listening there, what they were doing, they were broadcasting the news as seen from the Croatian side. Your know, along the lines of, Once again our troops are achieving victories on, you know, on this front and that front. You know, in the same way that when I listened to BiHTV in Sarajevo and elsewhere they would give the news from their particular perspective and, lo and behold, that also showed a large number of victories and it also pointed out the viciousness of the their opponents and they way that they were oppressing civilians, rather as the Croatian did. You know, I didn't take either news broadcast seriously. I regarded boat as propaganda. That was one of the reasons for the Western media being there, was to try to get to the truth of it and not take the slanted versions that were being broadcast by the protagonists in the war. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For the sake of our interpreters I do believe they need a break. We're going almost on two hours, and I don't mean -- I mean, I know the Prosecution has some questions and the gentleman wishes to go, but I think in fairness to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We're going to take a break and reconvene in 20 minutes' time. Mr. Praljak needs a few seconds to explain something, so when we reconvene we'll hear Mr. Praljak first for a few seconds, then the Prosecutor will be able to conclude the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak wants to clarify something. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like Mr. Bowen to look at the map. Can he please sign the map and put today's date. Secondly, in my decision pursuant to which BBC team is allowed to make their documentary, and this is where there was a mistake in the transcript, and I'm talking about Exhibit 3D 00700. It says precisely this, which is shooting a documentary in these areas. I would kindly like the interpreters to interpret this correctly: In these areas we are giving permission, and I interpret this means in all the areas under the control of the HVO and also permission to cross our check-points to the eastern side. I'm afraid there has been a different interpretation it, and I'm kindly asking for this to be established precisely. The permission applies to all areas, which means all areas under the control of the HVO. And the third thing I would like to clarify -- just a moment. Let me just finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please allow Mr. Praljak to finish what he was saying? Go ahead, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] And the third thing has to do with the voice and image synchronicity. When Mr. Bowen said the propaganda was not recorded well, and he said that to the interpreter, the interpreter was there every day. She could have recorded something better, and she could have underlaid that under the image. I would like to ask Mr. Bowen whether this is correct and whether this is technically possible to record a different sound and attach it to the image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, the interpretation issues. Mr. Praljak, can you read in your own language the text so the interpreters can interpret and then we can see what conclusions could be drawn. Can you please read in your own language the first paragraph. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] "Approval allowing free pass to the final check-point of the HVO military police on Buna to the BBC TV crew, the TV crew is making a documentary in these areas, in these areas."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you were on your feet?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Well, part of the answer has been -- I think part of the problem has been addressed. First of all, I guess, just so the record is -- there is no confusion in the record, when Mr. Praljak once again asked the witness to sign and date any of these items, I'd like the record to be clear as to what the significance is of signing it. What does that mean? The Chamber has given some indications before but I just want to make sure the record is clear of any significance of signing and dating the item. Number two, we now have the translation booth interpretation of the document. I don't think it's -- I don't think it's appropriate or acceptable, especially not in this context, for Mr. Praljak to get up and tell us what he thinks it really meant. I mean, the language is there. It's now been interpreted by the booth, and he cannot put his own spin on it as it were. I think those are where matters stand at the moment. Then I have a couple of questions, final questions, to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a map, sir, that you have before you. Could you please -- Mr. Praljak has -- which one, is it Mr. Praljak, the map on the left, the map on the right? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] The long map on the right-hand side of the witness. The witness has testified to the extent he could that this might have been the truthful representation. I'm not saying that the witness said that this was absolutely correct, but it says on the record to what extent the witness could confirm that this was the true representation, and that's why I'm asking him to sign the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, could you please sign the map. It is clear for the Trial Chamber the map has been shown to the witness. The questions have been asked, and he has answered the questions, which has been put on the record. Can we have the IC number for this Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will IC 247, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We're drawing to an end. Mr. Scott, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, when you were reporting as you told us about during your direct examination, when you were reporting of the events in Vukovar, can you just tell the Judges, please, who were the principal victims of the actions that were taking place around Vukovar at that time?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges, please, whether to your knowledge anyone on the Croat side complained about your reporting, that you didn't report the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object -- I object to the relevance and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you know that the Chamber, when a journalist makes a documentary, they rely on the reporting. We suppose that since the story has been aired on BBC there were people who applauded the story, and if we want to -- if we want to talk about this story, the Prosecution may ask whether there was any criticism about a certain documentary, and in this case we're talking about any Croatian criticism. Mr. Bowen, did you understand the question? We can assume that this story was also broadcast on TV, and, once it was broadcast, was there any criticism about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, there was criticism, Your Honour. It came from the Serb side. When I -- I travelled to the Serb side, I was actually held up at gunpoint and put in prison for -- or in a cell for some time because of their anger at our reporting of what was happening on the Croatian side. When I returned from -- from the Zagreb side, when I was -- during that period when I was going to Vukovar on a daily basis, they were very pleased that we were doing it because we were highlighting what was -- what was happening there. As I say, the only criticisms we had were from the Serbs who didn't like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, unfortunately, and, as you indicated yourself, your journalistic integrity has been somewhat attacked here. Could you tell the Judges when you pointed out -- when you heard that there were Croat prisoners on the Muslim side and when you asked and were allowed to film that, why did you want to include that?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was aware that using prisoners as forced labour on a front line, for example, as they were doing, was a war crime, and I was -- I'm always very interested in the -- the aspects of international humanitarian law that applied to the kind of things that I reported in war zones. I think it's a good way of putting them into context. So by using that framework of international humanitarian law. So I was -- and I think I made the point, I can't remember the precise words in the script, but, you know, I made the point that this was not a good thing to do. I can't remember if in the script or the documentary I used the word "war crimes," but anyway, the impression I was seeking to give was that this was a side that was fighting a war in a very determined, not to say ruthless, manner. You know, it was not my job, I felt, to say who were the good guys and who were the bad guys. My interest in war zones is more the effect of war on civilians rather than making judgements about who is in the right and who is in the wrong when they're actually fighting their war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As is suggested by the Defence that you were writing a pro-Muslim piece, did you think that that footage and what you saw and what was in your documentary, do you think that part of it reflected favourably on the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that it -- it -- well, it showed the reality -- you know, it showed the reality of what they were doing; it didn't show them in a particularly good light. In fact I said that in the script, I can see it now, that the commander didn't try to hide the way the Bosnian army treats its soldiers. "Prisoners dig the trenches and lay sandbags in the most exposed and dangerous positions on the front line." Now, I was not trying to make the Bosnian army out to be the good guys in this particular war. What I was most interested in was the condition and the plight and the pressure being put on 25.000 or so civilians who were in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bowen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to do some re-cross-examination. I'll be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber will deny you the right to put additional questions after the re-examination, and this is -- this has been the ruling of the Appeals Chamber. If you want to revisit some issues later on, there will be other witnesses, and they may be able to help you to clarify the things that you wanted to tackle today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Very well. But for the record, and I could care less what the Appeals Chamber has said about re-cross-examination. I am entitled to make the record. But I would ask the Trial Chamber to ask this gentleman here, when they sought permission supposedly and were denied permission from the commander of the HVO, which appears otherwise, did they -- did he mention Vukovar, that he had painted the Croats in a very positive way in Vukovar and therefore they would -- they should rest assured? Also, I would like the Trial Chamber, and this has not been mentioned by anyone, did he ever actually see this order that was by General Praljak and did he interpret it one way or another that he could not film anything, or was this -- was this told to him by the producer? In other words, did he actually see it and interpret it that they cannot do any filming on the west side of the river? Because I think those questions are left untouched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to rephrase this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, we have a problem about this decision or this -- decision by Mr. Praljak, and I'm going to put that question to you. When you had in your possession this decision that you were supposed to show at check-points that allowed you to move about, did you or any of your associates who were with you, I suppose that at that time that there were check-points, and if there were check-points you had to show the papers. So did you have that piece of paper on you, either you or some of your associates, to show at various check-points that you had to go through?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm assuming it was the same piece of paper. Yes. I was actually driving the vehicle, and so when we stopped at the HVO check-point I handed the piece of paper to the -- to the soldiers there. If I could just clarify just how you get these pieces of paper in these situations. They tend to be -- you get the paper after the discussion, and then someone says to you -- you have your negotiation, you have your discussion, they gave you the answer, and then they gave you a piece of paper that you hope will cover the agreement that you've made. That's the way it always worked. You get it after the end of your meeting, as it were. You hang around for a bit. They go off and type it, and then they come back and you go out with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In English I see that you say, "I handed the piece of paper." Did you read it? When you heard that there was a document, did you read it or did you just take it for granted that you had a piece of paper that would get you through?

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yeah, I had a look at t I is a you that all our names were on it, see that Matthews' name has been misspelt, but it -- I mean, I can't read Croatian. I had a limited knowledge of the language. Maybe a vocabulary of about a hundred words that I used to use at check-points and I certainly couldn't read it or write it. And our interpreter explained to me that this was the pass that would get us through the HVO check-point, and we certainly didn't interpret it as something that gave us authority to film on both sides, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was the gentleman at the negotiations? That's the critical aspect of it. And I think that's what needs to be said. Now, from his previous as I understand it, he was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that you have already answered, Mr. Bowen, and that you said that you were not involved in that. It was your colleague Matthews who was involve in the negotiations. That's what I understood. Maybe I have misunderstood. When Mr. Praljak handed you that document, had you participated in those negotiations, or was it Mr. Matthews who was involved and who was in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: JEREMY BOWEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, you explained it correctly. I was not at those negotiations, as I made clear several times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's exactly what I understood, and that's why I have not asked you to clarify. Your testimony is now finished. It was very long. It lasted almost two days. I would like to thank you on behalf of myself and my colleagues for having answered the questions by the Prosecution, by the Defence teams, the accused, and the Judges. I wish you a safe journey back home, and I wish you success in your journalistic career. I'm going to ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the next witness, it has been indicated that the Prosecution will have two hours. I believe that there is a video that will last about an hour, so together the Prosecution will have two hours including the video, and the Defence teams will have the same amount of time for the cross-examination. So once the Prosecution finishes, we should then finish the cross-examination tomorrow at 7.00. Is that the way you have foreseen things for this week, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. Apparently there's been some confusion. The video has nothing to do with the next witness. The video we have put on the schedule some days ago when the schedule was circulated to everyone, including to the Judges, and as further explained in a letter that should have been distributed to you today and to counsel. This is the presentation of various video material. The Chamber, and in particular yourself, Mr. President, has invited us on a number of occasions to present video material to the Chamber, and we're prepared to do that tomorrow. But it has nothing to do specifically with this witness. When the next witness is finished, we would propose to play that video material, which is approximately one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to understand. There is a witness who is forthcoming?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there is a video, the video will be shown to the witness so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the video has nothing to do with the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. There is no connection between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now I understand much better. There is no connection between the two. Very well. For your examination-in-chief of this witness, how much time will you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Two hours, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two hours. And after the cross-examination, the video that has nothing to do with the witness will have to be played tomorrow, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It can be played any time, Your Honour. Obviously if we don't finish the witness until 7.00 tomorrow night we won't have the video tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe just a minute about that video that has been announced. We have received a notification today from the Prosecution and the script of all the videotapes that the Prosecution wants to show without any witnesses, in the absence of any witnesses. I have not had time to consult with my colleagues; however, on behalf of General Praljak's Defence I object to these videos being shown in such short time. We simply don't have time to view all that material, and as you've just said, it will not be shown tomorrow. It will not be possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, I'm surprised. This material is P 1041, and it was disseminated already a month ago. First of all, you had to watch the video when you got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not talking about the video that we had for the previous witness. We're talking about the letter dated 24 January, which is today, in which the Prosecutor informs us that tomorrow they want to show 9 or 11 video clips. In the absence of any witnesses, I object to that. It can't be done from one day to another. We have to have the time to view the videotapes that are to be shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you have just entered the courtroom, and I want to ask you a question. After this witness we are going to have a video, a video that consists of several tapes, and the numbers are 1041, 2059, 2463, 242 -- all these videotapes, can you tell us when were they disclosed to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I will continue to handle this particular matter please. Your Honour, these are -- as the Court has just rightly pointed out, all of these are exhibits in the 65 ter exhibit list, and we had indicated some -- that we would be playing videos. What they -- what they are is that from these various videos there has been put together, approximately a one-hour presentation and again, Your Honour, we've done that with the understanding that this is what the Chamber has asked us to do. If the Chamber doesn't want to hear it, doesn't want to receive it that way, of course you can tell us that, but that's -- again we're going forward on the basis of your direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Since the Judges will meet tomorrow as they indeed meet every day, we will discuss this issue and tomorrow we will be able to tell you what will happen with this video presentation, but we have to tell you that we have noted the objection of the Defence that has informed us that they have not been given enough time to prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, before you read the solemn declaration could you please stand up. You're going to tell me your name, your first name, last name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jovan Rajkov, born August 26, 1957.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a doctor, a surgeon, and I work in the South Camp hospital in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, have you ever testified before an International Tribunal or a local court about the events that took place in your country in the 1990s of last century or is this the first time you testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read the solemn declaration that the usher is just giving to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Doctor. You may be seated. Since this is the first time you are appearing before a court as a witness, I'm going to provide you with some information as to how this testimony of yours is going to take place. First of all, you're going to be asked questions by the Prosecution whom you may have met today or yesterday. The Prosecution has informed us that they will need two hours for the examination-in-chief, and during their examination, I'm sure that they will be showing you some documents. They have provided us with a bundle of documents which is about half a metre wide. When they have finished with their examination it will be the Defence's turn. They are seated to your left. As you can see there are a number of them. Behind them are the six accused who are also entitled to put questions within the scope of what we call the cross-examination. We have issued a decision to give ample time to Defence for their cross-examination. Your testimony should finish tomorrow by 7.00 in the afternoon. Please try and be as precise as possible in your answers, because your answers are being translated into the English language, and that -- you can see on the screen before you constitute the transcript, and we will also have some evidence in the form of documents that will be presented to you by the Prosecution and the Defence. The four Judges seated before you can at any point in time ask you questions according to our Rules, and we will certainly take that opportunity either to clarify some of your answers or to clarify some things to us, because it is our task in the future when this trial is adjourned to deliberate and to render a decision in these proceedings. If during your testimony there are any problems, please do not hesitate to inform us about that, especially if you are not feeling well, because even though you are a doctor, sometimes it does happen that witnesses don't feel well, and we would like you to inform us about that as soon as possible. This is how all this should take place, but I believe that the Prosecutor has already informed you about all this. I'm now going to give the floor to Ms. Egels for the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Witness, could you briefly describe to the Trial Chamber what is your professional background from approximately 1989 until April 1993, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: As you mentioned 1989, by then I had completed the secondary school and the faculty of medicine in Sarajevo. I passed my professional examinations and started working as a volunteer or doing temporary work for 15 days, up to a month, in the emergency unit. I worked in the emergency clinic from 1989 to 1992 with a few interruptions because it was all temporary work, but as a volunteer I was present all the time up until 1989. And you want to know after that, do you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Yes, until April 1993, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: From the 11s of April to the 11th of June I worked in the military unit. On the 11th of June, Dr. Dzikic, who was the head at the time, said he didn't need my services any more, and I tried to activate myself, not to stay at home doing nothing. Since I was a doctor I joined up with the civilian protection, but I wasn't registered with the civilian protection I was just there and did everything that I could and knew how to do until - I don't know what day this was - when a list appeared with some 19 Serb names and surnames and three Muslim names on it. This list was posted and both times under both lists on one piece of paper it said that the people listed were required to leave the premises of the civilian protection doesn't, and I logically concluded that the best thing for me to do would be to leave because I didn't know what this -- what was going on and what this was about. So I stayed at home for a certain amount of time until I linked up with the BH army through private channels. And from the 27th of August, 1992, I became a doctor within the Medical Corps of the BH army and the Mostar battalion. And that was until 1992. When the Medical Corps relocated from where it was to begin with in South Camp and the south barracks in Mostar, we relocated mostly because I insisted on having a better -- better premises, and I went to the hygiene institute. That was in October 1992. And that's where I stayed until May 1993 when that hospital, it was a hospital, and it really started working as a hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Let me take you back. You just explained to us that you went to the hygiene institute from October 1992 onwards. There is a map that is going to be provided to you that has Exhibit number 9517. Can I ask you to show us on that map where the hygiene institute is? Can I ask you to mark the location of the hygiene institute with number 1, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: If I may say so, this isn't a very precise map. So -- and I don't think some of the small streets have been entered into it properly. It's difficult to orientate oneself. Let me just take a moment to do that. And you want a number there, do you?

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Number 1 for the hygiene institute, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to this map P 9717, many witnesses made the same remarks and said that it was very difficult to find their way there and that some of the street names had changed. Isn't it possible for the Prosecution to find a map of Mostar dated 1993? I assume that you can't give me a reply now, but as professional Judges this is something that came to my mind straight away.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Your Honour, a complete answer is indeed not something that I can give you, but what I can tell you is that indeed it was very difficult to find an accurate map of 1993 of Mostar except for the military maps, but the military maps are being so detailed that then we are facing the other problem, which is to try to find a simple street back on that map. So this is why we chose this commercial map to try to give a certain idea of what it looked like. Now, maybe for the purpose of this specific location --

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us, the hygiene institute, on which street was it located?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: If I might be allowed to add something. On this area below this separation line there were no changes in the street names. The street names remained the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak wanted to say something about the map. He was on his feet. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] On the glass behind you, Witness, we have a very detailed map, an aerial view of Mostar. So perhaps you can use that one so that we have the precise locations marked on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Well, I believe that for the purpose of this location the witness just marked the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Can you just give us the name of the street where the hygiene institute was, please?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: The street in which the institute was and where it is now is called Marsal Tito Street or Main Street, and it is in fact the main street.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And is this street located in East or in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: East.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you explained that you entered the ABiH and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have an IC number first, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but I was going to ask that a little bit later because I was going to ask the witness to mark other locations on the map, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could have a number because it will be simpler. A number Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be given Exhibit number IC 248, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: So you explained to us you entered the ABiH and you started first as a doctor, first at the south camp, then at the hygiene institute, and this until April of 1993. Now, to take you back to that period of April of 1993, was then a war hospital established in the location of the hygiene institute in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: You can't call it the establishment of a war hospital -- a hospital, especially not a war hospital. Those of us that were there of the medical service, there were 3 times 6 of us, six doctors, six nurses, six drivers. We relocated the -- well, clinic or outpatients' clinic from south camp to the hygiene institute where we used the basement section. Only the left-hand side, a very small room there for -- as a reception for the patients, a small room where they spent the day, and a small medicines depot. And one of the rooms was supposed to be for the dentist, but that was never actually finished. We never had the necessary equipment. That's what we managed to do, but perhaps in April, moving towards May, thanks to the fact that we left the right-hand side empty if the need arose for -- that right side had some rooms which had tiles on the walls, and there was a trough for washing, as we call it, a trough with two or three taps, and two old sterilisation pieces of equipment which the hygiene institute used, then we thought that this would be ideal for emergencies, as an operating theatre. And there were other rooms there that could be used if we came by the equipment we needed equipment -- we were general practitioners, so we had an idea of what an operations unit theatre should look like, so we managed to collect that equipment and we had something that resembled an operating theatre, at least under those conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, there seems to be a divergence between what you're saying and what the Prosecution is saying. The Prosecution termed this presence as a war hospital and you said no it was just a hygiene institute with additional equipment as a surgery. Now, was this a civilian or a military facility? And the personnel there, including yourself, were you civilians or were you under military statute?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning in 1992 to 1993, it was a surgery and later on became a war hospital. It was a surgery or clinic organised by the BH army and, yes, the staff did come under the authority, if I can put it that way, of certain commands. I'm not a military expert, so I don't know about the chain of command, but during the war everything seems to be under some sort of military command. But if you're asking me whether it was only soldiers who were treated there, then no. The entire population on the east bank, civilians, women, children, everybody without any difference were treated there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So did you have -- were you a civilian or were you a military man working, or were you a civilian working in a military hospital? What was your status?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally did have a military ID card as of August 1992, and that was the only way at the time that you could be on the east bank unless you were in -- an inhabitant of the east bank. Unless you had a house there you had to have permission to cross over to that side. I lived on the west bank, so if you were a member and had this ID card, then you could cross over to the other bank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That gives us a little more insight. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit number 9865. It is in the three binders that are just next to you, and it's in the last binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise the building on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: Certainly I do. That is the hygiene institute in Mostar in Tito Street taken later on. And the building was a different colour then. It was purple.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Witness, could you show us on that picture, and maybe by using the picture on the screen in front of you, where the medical part of that hospital was first based in that building? Can we see that on this picture? You talk about the basement of the building.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: You want me to show you the medical part. It's not really a basement, a cellar. Not everything is below ground, and you can see that here. That is the level of the basement ceiling. So the basement ceiling was on that level. So a third of it was above ground. There's a window, as you can see. That's the window over there. At the beginning, what I mentioned to begin with, this area here was the room that -- well, we used it as a kitchen. We used it as a day room. And the reception area was on the opposite side. I can't show you that here. There's a separate entrance on the other side, on the back side of this building. So when you go down the steps into a small room, on the same level of all this was the reception area where we took patients in. The medicines -- where we kept the medicines was on the other side. And the room that became the operating theatre is here, under this area here, right along the length of the building. And then the intensive care unit was next to the operating theatre. So that was it basically.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Could I ask registry to give an IC number to this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be given Exhibit number IC 249, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Witness, in April 1993, by whom was the rest of the building occupied? The upper floors of the building.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: In April 1993, you mean? Well, I have to explain it this way: When we arrived into the building as a medical corps, we were sort of tenants, not to say guests, of the 1st Customs Company which used this building for its own purposes. As far as I could see during that period it wasn't actually used for anything else but a premises to rest in or somewhere where they would gather when they were sent on assignment up at the front line. There was a small room at the entrance looking onto the main street. It was the communications centre, if I can call it that, with the special telephone and flippers and so on. But they didn't use the building all the time. They used it when they liked. But they gave the whole basement area over to us. They remained on the floor above, and little by little they left the building until the whole building came to be used as a hospital, and later on there were hospital rooms for patients on the upper storey.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: In April of 1993 was the whole building already used for medical purposes?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: In April, no, the whole building wasn't used for medical purposes, just part of the basement area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Moving further into the period of May of 1993, was at that time the building used only for medical purposes?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: If you want me to tell you exactly, I know what happened on the 9th of May. Later on things went step-by-step, but on the 9th of May, 1993, we used, and I'll enumerate all the things, the reception surgery. That is to say the little room to the left of the staircase. The day room, the dispensary that I mentioned for the storing of medicines, the operating theatre, and the room next door where there were seven or eight beds at the most on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: On the 9th of May, 1993, were there any soldiers accommodated in that building from the company you mentioned? Were there any weapons gathered in that building?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: On the 9th of May there was still someone up on the storey above. We hadn't taken over that floor for our medical purposes, and they would just go there to have a bit of a rest, a lie-down and so on. Now, before we took over all of it they stored some weapons, a little -- a small amount of weapons in the basement room. They were asked to get rid of them, so on the 9th of May, that wasn't there any longer. Where they moved those weapons I don't know. It wasn't within the compound of that building. So there wasn't any of that after the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Witness, as we are now on the 9th of May, I would just like to take you to that specific date. Could you tell us about the situation on that specific date as you remember it from where you were at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: I can start a few days before that, if that isn't a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Yes. Go on.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: Here's why -- let me tell you why. Because I came on duty -- we had 24-hour duty shifts. I arrived on duty on the 6th of May, and already at that time -- well, like the people like to say there was tension. The situation in town was tense. It was dangerous to move around in a uniform by another army group, if you were to pass by somebody else. That's the impression I gave. But I went to work wearing civilian clothes. I was on duty on the 6th of May, and on the 7th in the morning, that was customary, we would hand over a report to the chief of the medical service. Rahmo was the man. I think he was in the command buildings in Vranica, wherever. I don't know. Anyway, I phoned him up in the morning, reported to him, and he told me that the situation was tense and that it would be better if I stayed there and tell the people taking up shifts after me, that they should stay there on the 6th, 7th, and 8th of May. During that time we had an awful lot of work. They said quite clearly although nothing specific was stated they just said the situation was tense, highly tense, you knew you had to prepare for something but you didn't know exactly what because nobody specified. So I always had the impression that things were spontaneous and it was just thanks to the people employed there to -- that were working there, that we had to work quickly to equip the premises that we wanted to have and to use as a -- as a theatre, operating theatre. So -- and the dispensary and so on. We selected the types of medicines we needed for emergencies, for large numbers of injured or wounded persons if something was going to happen. And obvious -- we sort of felt that it probably was. And I know that on the 9th of -- on the 8th of May in the afternoon Dr. Konjhodzic came by and he asked me -- he said, "Should I be here today or not?" I asked him where he lived. He said he lived in Ledara, which I knew was somewhere on the border regions, the border belt between the BH army and the HVO, and I told him to come. So he came around at some - at about 5.00 a.m., laid down on the bed next to me, and then some terrible shelling started. There was a lot of terrible firing and shooting, and we thought, What's happening, nobody told us anything. We switched the radio on. There were some proclamations which sort of said that an operation was under way by the HVO and the police forces, I'm paraphrasing now, of course, and that members of the BH army were asked to surrender, to hand over their weapons, and to put out white flags of surrender. And in the meantime songs, patriotic songs were being played, you could hear them, and the wounded began coming in. And then there was, what can I call it, a semi-organised chaos in the hospital because it was a hospital. As soon as you begin getting in a large number of patients needing surgery, it was no longer an outpatients' department or anything like that. You had to deal with them and operate. You had to tend to the wounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: So on that -- sorry. On that first day, on the 9th of May, were there any casualties brought to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Straight away in the morning. Well, not at 5.00 a.m., no. People didn't know where to be -- where to drive or take the wounded. But it's a small town, so by word of mouth people began to realise where these people should be taken. So around 8.00 or 9.00 we received our first casualty, fatality. He was a soldier lying face down on a stretcher, and the second person to be killed after that one was a nurse of ours. She was 19. Her name was Linda Petkovic. And I know that she was one of those darkers, darker types that launched herself into any risky situation that was around, and she went to the main road with an ambulance and a driver. It was a sort of white Italian ambulance that they managed to pick up. And we heard that the vehicle was hit -- when they were coming back from Konak, that they were targeted and hit by an anti-aircraft machine-gun. The driver was wounded, but Linda was the second fatality. On that day we had 14 fatalities. It wasn't a problem for me to remember that. Fourteen people dead. I don't know why I had -- was told to do something with the bodies, and I put them into an empty room up there on the floor above, and I know that quite literally I lined them all up and that there were 14 of them, and there was nowhere elsewhere I could put them except on the floor. So I lined them up along the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: When you refer to the death of Linda the nurse, and you said she was in an ambulance, was the vehicle distinctively marked as an ambulance?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was what we call the ambulance, emergency ambulance, yes. It wasn't an ordinary kombi van or anything like that. It was an ambulance for emergency.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And when these first casualties came in, was there anyhow [sic] that the name or diagnosis of these people were documented at that time on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: Well, some records were kept of patients. They were introduced into the logbook that the surgery used. There wasn't a separate logbook that was kept as of that first day, but it letter the logbook well. It was just the last pages of the logbook we'd been using previously there, in the surgery. Now, how precisely they were kept well, we can discuss it, why they're like they are, incomplete, because of all the conclusion that reigned in the hospital at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a question from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Madam Prosecutor, but I'd just like to seek clarification, to clear up the confusion in my mind. Your hospital began taking in persons who were wounded, how were injured, but before you said that, there were soldiers there and they had weapons in the basement as of the 8th of May. Is that right? While you were -- were the soldiers still there? And what about the weapons? Were the weapons still there when these casualties began coming in? Could you clear that up for me, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think you heard everything I said. Probably that's the case. On that day there were no weapons in that building. I know that because I know that that particular room where the weapons had previously been stored -- not that they were taken away on the 8th of May, they were taken away before the 9th of May on some day, but I know when I -- when we were there in the basement premises, on one occasion I happened to see that room open, and I saw that there were some weapons in there, when we arrived at the beginning. And we demanded that the weapons be taken away. They needed a little time to do that, to find where to take the weapons. Where they took them, I don't know, but it wasn't moved to anywhere else in the building because I knew every nook and cranny of that house. I knew every corner of that building and I knew there were no weapons in the hospital. Not then, no. That's for sure. Now, as far as the soldiers were concerned, I said that by that time they had given over the basement to us. Yes, some of them used some of the rooms above to rest or just to pass the time. Some of them. Let me explain that. It's a building which sort of belonged to the 1st Customs Company, and members of that company were people who lived in the surrounding neighbourhood. And if you look at the map, you'll be able to see, if you can see - I don't know, can you see? - that the hygiene institute is in part of town by is called Carina. Carina. So it was the 1st Carina company, Carina meaning customs. So the hygiene institute was in a part of down called Carina. Can we show it here? Can you see that? And soldiers lived in houses nearby, so they didn't need to stay in that building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: To go back to the previous question, you explained that the casualties that came in on the 9th of May were recorded in a protocol book. Can I ask you to turn to Exhibit number P 02789, and it's in the first binder just next to you. 2789. It's that first document, 278 -- 6, sorry. Sir, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: I know what this is. This is one of the last pages of the previously mentioned protocol book which had been used by the surgery up until the 9th of May, and until then we thought of it as the protocol of the war hospital, and I know that because there is something very characteristic on that particular page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: The patient number 5 on the list 4545 is Bajrami Hidajeta. He was born in 1976. Let me translate what it says on the right-hand side. She was a pregnant lady just about to give birth to her child. I know that she arrived on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you to explain how to read this protocol book starting by the first column.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Your Honour, I apologise to my learned friend. We have a wrong document on e-court. Just to avoid any confusion. We don't have the same document on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: So the document is P 02786.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: So as I said, could I ask you to explain to us how to read this document starting from the first column with the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: The first column contains numbers, but there is something before that. There's the markings that were adopted into our practice in the war hospital in order to simplify things and in order to incorporate as much information as possible, because the only records that we could have and we could keep were this type of protocol books. Why I'm saying this. These are not our hospital protocols. We used the protocols that we could get hold of. The one that we are looking at had previously been used by the outpatients surgery of the former JNA. That you can see at the top of the page, because it says "Rank, military post." We squeezed everything on one page in order to record as much as possible. The basic things, that is, the basic things were the name, the date of birth, and the diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, let's clarify a few mention. Can you comment upon the first thing that we can see column by column? On the left-hand side there is a square, a black square. There is a P, and so on and so forth. Can you take it little by little and explain every single thing? What are these things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. On circled P is the initial or the first letter in the word "reception," which means that the patient was admitted. Then there's an ordinal number in the protocol from the moment the protocol was opened up to that moment. Then there is the first and the last names of the patient. You can see that, can't you? Then there is the year of birth. The first one is 1968. Then there is an empty space. And then there is a diagnosis. And I can read the diagnosis to you, the first one. I can translate it to you, if you want me to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just the first one. What was the diagnosis for the first patient?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The diagnosis for the first patient when you read it in Latin, when you read the abbreviation, this is vulnera explosiva, thoraxis et abdominis, which means, they there, this is multiple wound, these were almost all wounds, and, if it is VV, then it means multiple wounds, explosive wounds of the right side of the chest and of the right arm. That's for the first patient. Later on there are some other data, which are important to explain for you to understand what they mean, and I can go on and explain them to you, the information and data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The third patient that you can see on this page, number 4543. His number's encircled. We did that in order to show who died, who had been killed, and the lethal outcome. For example, if anywhere in the protocol the number is encircled, that means that the person died. Then there is the name and the family name. There is no age, no year of birth. We could not find that out. We -- it says that he is a soldier. We sometimes put that, whether somebody was a soldier, a civilian, or a child. Why a child? Because we wanted to know whether there was a certain person in question because some people share the same names. It says here "soldier." There is also a diagnosis, vulnera explosiva, thoraxis et abdominis, which means explosive wounds of the chest, abdomen, and it says "exit lethalis," which means lethal outcome at 13 hours 20 minutes. The circle is just to facilitate reading the protocol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the last qualification. Those who recorded these things, were they doctors, nurses, paramedics, military, civilians? Who were those who worked in the protocol? It seems that this is the same handwriting so it must have been the same person. But who were these people who filled out the protocol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is the same handwriting, but the principle was this: The diagnoses were established and filled out by doctors. Here you can see that in this particular case the doctor also entered all the other information, the name, the last name, the date of birth, the diagnosis, everything. Later on, as the hospital developed and as we had an increased number of cases, an increased number of wounded, it depended on the shift, who the people on the shift were, who was the official person on duty, although we did everything during the period of time that was necessary for the work to be completed. We somehow divided work in the way it was suitable to the shift. In our -- my shift we had a paramedic who in realistic terms was a doctor, because he was just about to graduate from the medical school. So if we had 14 patients at the same time, this is how we did: He would record the names. I would establish the diagnosis. I would make a note of that on a piece of paper, and then together with him I would coordinate the names with the wounds. That's why in certain cases you can find two different handwritings of that person and of another very experienced paramedic. So in some cases these two paramedics would sometimes write, "diagnosis pursuant to our instructions." A diagnosis otherwise should not have been entered by a paramedic. It was always our diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is now 20 to 6.00. We're going to have a 20-minute break and we shall resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall now resume. I believe we have to give an IC number to a document. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The handwritten schematic drawing of the Neretva banks shall be given Exhibit number IC 250. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This has lasted five seconds, and this is how it should be done. Please proceed, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Witness, to go back to the exhibit that we were just looking at before the break, 2786, you mentioned as a diagnosis at the first line, "v explosiva." Could you give us the basic diagnosis of war wounds that we can find back in such protocols?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: I'm not -- I can say it's very simple. There is explosive wounds and gunshot wounds. The explosive wounds are inflicted by explosive devises as a result of shell -- explosion, booby-trap explosions and gunshot wounds which could be divided into two wounds. Those are penetration wounds, penetration -- gunshot wounds as a result of a bullet. And then there's penetration wound which have the entry point and the exit point, again gunshot wounds which have penetrated the body and have left the body through a different point, through the exit point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would that qualification result from the international standards on distinguishing between different types of wounds inflicted by various types of explosives and bullets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is some of discrepancy among experts in the field to a certain extent, and I'll tell you what this is about. Every -- it has always been a question whether a wound is inflicted by a bullet that explodes in the body, and there are such wounds, and I know that from the war experience. Sometimes a bullet enters the body and then its brass casing explodes into several fragments in the body. In practice, if you don't have a complete set of diagnostic devices such as ATG, which allows you to see whether the wound was inflicted by the shrapnel or whether it -- the wound was inflicted by the -- a brass casing. If there are many fragments, it is always a question what the wound was inflicted by. However, in practice a gunshot wound is always inflicted by a bullet, by a pistol bullet, a rifle bullet, or any type of bullet, whether it remained intact, in one piece, or whether it was fragmented. This is at least what -- what you can find in forensic textbooks that I and my colleagues used to learn from. This is what our diagnoses are based on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And in these protocol books, Witness, these explosive wounds and gunshot wounds, how are they mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: In -- in interpretation I don't quite get your question. Can the interpretation be a bit more clear so that I can answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: When one reads the diagnosis in these protocol books, is the -- are the words, for instance, "Explosive wound," or "Gunshot wound" written in your language or is it written in another language, and if it is written in another language, what are the words used for these two specific kind of wounds?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: In our medical practice the diagnoses are always in Latin, if I understand your question correctly. So these are not descriptions of the wounds. These are Latin terms for the types of wounds. Everything is in Latin.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: So what would be the Latin term for explosive wound?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: Vulnus explosivum.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And what would be the Latin term for gunshot wound?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: Vulnus sclopetarium or transsclopetarium, if it is a penetration wound with an entry and exit point. So we're talking about two types of gunshot or sclopetarium wounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you. Flipping through the document that you have in front of you, do you at one point recognise your own handwriting in that document?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: It's not easy to find. This is a minimised copy of the original that is somewhat larger. For example, here, 416 is 0. The diagnosis is in my handwriting, but the name is not, however. 4630 is -- the name is in my handwriting whereas the diagnosis not. 4602. This is my happened writing. The complete entry save for the therapy that is mentioned here. And there is a lot more of that if you wish me to continue. And these pages I can't see any more. 4613, as well the name, diagnosis, and therapy, they're all in my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. To go back to the 9th of May and the situation in the hospital, in the days afterward how did the situation unfold at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: On the first day we had one major problem. Those were patients that had to be surgically treated. We had a young lad. I remember that he was wounded in the upper leg, and he was wounded in his genitals. He had to be surgically treated. However, what we could do was to try and do it in local anaesthesia, because the only doctor who was present there and who had some surgical knowledge and who was of that speciality was Dr. Konjhodzic, who fortunately enough was also a general surgeon and a neurosurgeon. He had two specialties. However, we did not have an anaesthesiologist, so we could not anaesthetise the patient. Between the night of the 10th of May we treated him surgically but in local anaesthesia, which was not pleasant for the patient nor for us. And especially not for me. I was just a beginner. I was a general practitioner at the time. What we managed to do on the following days by asking questions, by making inquiries with all those who arrived was to try and ask them and find somebody in the town who would be either a surgeon or an anaesthesiologist, and we managed to bring to the hospital an anaesthesiologist, and that was the only anaesthesiologist that we that we ever had in the hospital, and we also brought another surgeon. So maybe within the next 48 hours we had an anaesthesiologist, two surgeons, and the four of us who had worked before in the outpatients' clinic. Three of us were general practitioners, and the fourth person was a dentist. If you want me to tell you something else, I would like to say that during the first few days we were forced to take over from the army the rooms upstairs one by one because we needed beds and rooms for the patients. The total number of beds that we managed to put into the hospital -- why I'm saying managed, because there was simply not enough room for all that we needed. And I know that we had 13 beds in the so-called ICU, which was the room next to the operating theatre. There were actually two rooms by the OR, and we also used beds in front of the OR. There were 13 such beds. Upstairs there were 2 times 13 beds, in other words 26 beds all together and plus the 13 downstairs, that was the top capacity of that building. That was the building filled to the full. And during those first days or within the first week we were forced to discharge patients after only a few days to some other premises in town which were not even close to being equipped as our hospital. But there was room for the patients, and that was the most important thing. They could be hospitalised there, although this was not real hospitalisation, but they were under our care, under the care of medical personnel even there, even in those improvised rooms.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: You just mentioned other premises. Could you tell us what premises you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: The buildings I'm talking about usually bear the names that they used to have before the war. I'm primarily referring to the -- what we called stationary, which had been used in the army for a place where military patients, recruits, conscripts were hospitalised. For example, they could not be for the active service or for the hospital. If they had a sore throat then they would be placed in something that whereas something like an outpatient clinic. So we used the same term. For example, let me try and remember, to start with, from north to the south. One was in the atomic shelter in Zalik. Another such premise was in the building across the road from --

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you and ask you to go back to the map of Mostar that you were showed a little bit before, and that is now bearing IC number 248, and maybe pinpoint on that map the locations you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: Shall I just point to them or shall I mark them? This is a very thick felt-tip pen, so it's not easy for me to mark.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: May we just mark them with a pen and with a number. So the first you just mentioned was -- the atomic shelter in Zalik will bear a number 2 for that map.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: Can you hear me? I can do it just by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If number 1 is outpatients' clinic, now we need number 2 to mark the next thing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, number 2 can just be an approximation because Zalik is not on the map because it is further to the north-east from the boundaries of the map. I can just point to the direction. I can just mark the direction where Zalik was. Shall I go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next one would be the building across the road which did not have an official name. It was just called the building across the road. It was not a building. It was just a facility that was under construction. It had just the back walls, some columns, and the upper floor, and the concrete ceiling. Fortunately enough it had a basement. And it was in use until the moment when the basement was flooded. And that -- it was just across the road from the hygiene institute, and I can mark it on the map. The next one --

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: This is number 3.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: The next such building was the premises of the former insurance company called Dunav. I'll try and find it here on the map. Shall I put number 4 next to it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: There it is, number 4. That's the Dunav. And the next one, further to the south, is in the basement of the former social security services, which is in Fejiceva Street. Again, this is just an approximation. So this is number 5. And the next such building toward the south which had been used until the moment the building was hit and burnt down, but nothing happened to anybody in there. This is the former building of the League of Communists that they used to refer to as the committee building. That's number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: 6, yes.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: [Marks]. The next such building is the former health centre in Brankovac. This is a large building. At the beginning we used only the basement, and then we were forced to use other floors as well to the extent possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: In all of these buildings what was the extent of the facilities and the equipment for the patients?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: There was no equipment as such. Let me tell you why. The patients were there in beds such as they existed, and as for the personnel there was a nurse in each of the buildings, and they would change shifts. What they had, they had dressing material and some pain-killers. They didn't have any instruments or anything else. And a doctor would be given a task from time to time which depended on the situation and on the status of the patients. A doctor would be given a task to visit some of these buildings, to check up on the patients and to intervene if necessary. According to the plan that the patients were given, patients would either come to us or would be brought to us to have their wounds dressed. This would happen during the night when it was safer. Our situation was somewhat different in Zalik, in the vicinity of the Zalik facility because a doctor resided there. He was in charge of that facility. And in the Brankovac facility, maybe a few weeks later we had to accommodate the department of internal medicine because we had patients with heart conditions and similar things. And the hygiene institute had to be dedicated to surgery. So maybe 15 days later in Brankovac we had doctors who were only in charge of internal medicine patients with internal diseases. And since we also brought surgical patients to recover there, then these patients as well would be in their charge, in the charge of those specialists in internal medicine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, if I understand you well, you're saying that number 1 was the facility where there were three surgeons, two GPs, and this is where you received all those who had been wounded or killed. They were treated there on the spot. They were surgically treated. And then after that you would dispatch them to the six other facilities. And Brankovac was a more specialised facility with a specialist in internal medicine. And you're saying that in other places there was very little. There was some dressing material and a few medicines. But the surgical team were primarily located in the facility number 1. And you're saying that during the night those who had been dispatched to the six buildings could return to the facility number 1 to have their wounds dressed and tended to. Is that what the situation was like in medical terms, and is that what the situation was like with regard to the facilities that you had at your disposal to treat the wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is precisely so. In the institute, hygiene institute, there was an anaesthesiologist, two surgeons, and four GPs. This is what I said, and as for the patients being brought to us, this was our plan, which didn't always succeed. It depended on the situation. Those who had to be additionally treated were brought back if they needed a minor surgery or surgical treatment of the wound. If that was too dangerous, then this would be either postponed or the fashion would be changed. They wouldn't come to us. We would rather go to them. We would go across the road or to some other facility, if that's what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have explained that these facilities received both soldiers and civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If a child, for example, suffered from an appendix, where would they be sent? Where would such a child be sent, to you or to one of those other facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These children would be sent to the hygiene institute.
