Any patient who needed surgical treatment would be taken straight to the hygiene institute, but on one occasion I personally had an occasion to provide CPR to a man who had a heart failure. So if you're asking me about any surgical cases, all of them were brought to us, be it a hernia or an appendicitis, any such case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you I have understood. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Sir, except for the hygiene institute and the other institutes you've referred to were there any other institutes in Mostar after 9 May, and, if so, which ones?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: There were others. At first we referred to them as points and then as outpatients' clinics. Why? Because it was impossible for anybody to move from one part of the town to the other, from south to the centre, from Zalik to the hygiene institute. If you wanted to go on foot it was very far, and that's why we set up the so-called outpatients' clinic in certain places that I can identify for you, or I can even mark those for you, but I don't know whether you'll be able to orientate yourself on the map. I would very much like to have another pen in order to be more precise when marking. This is very thick, a very thick tip. Shall I mark? In the Zalik shelter there was an outpatient clinic manned by Dr. Duranovic. I suppose I don't have to mark that again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: In Santic Street -- not exactly in Santic Street because Santic Street was the combat line, the closest to it was this outpatients' clinic which was referred to as Santic outpatient clinic. It was somewhere around here. What number should I mark it with, number 8? It was between a wall and the counter of a former bakery. That was where the outpatients' clinic was. In Cernica -- in the shelter of a residential building, there was the Cernica outpatient clinic. In the so-called Semovac there was another outpatients' clinic. That's number 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: So just for the record because while you're marking it it's not recorded, the Cernica outpatient clinic was given number 9; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Okay. And Semovac number 10?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Along the front line there were three outpatients' clinics, 8, 9 and 10. Very quickly, what was the medical equipment in those outpatients' clinics? Was there a nurse? Was there a doctor? Who was there, and what did they have by way of medical equipment? Because they were very close to the front line, and this -- these were the places that -- where they might have victims to which they had to tend very quickly. What did they have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll tell you as soon as I show you where another outpatients' clinic was, which was in Donja Mahala, number 11. And I am adjust repeating. This is just approximations hereabouts. Each of these outpatients' clinics had its doctor on staff. Those were all general practitioners. Those were doctors who resided in the vicinity of these outpatients' clinics. I can tell you their names, if you wish me to do so, if it's important. In Zalik, the doctor who worked there was a doctor who lived in a building not far from the outpatients' clinic. In Santiceva, a doctor worked who lived in a building next to that outpatients' clinic. In Cernica there was a doctor who had previously resided in the west side but then was expelled, and that is where he resided at the moment. And as for Semovac and Mahala, we had one doctor who -- whose house was in between the two of these outpatients' clinics. There were also nurses who were not officially employed. We used the former students of the medical high school who had not completed their education, but they had basic medical knowledge, and they had some basic dressing materials. They didn't have any surgical tools or instruments. They did not perform any surgical procedures. They would refer patients to us. And they had some basic medicines that we managed to donate to them from our central dispensary. And I'm talking about pain-killers, some antibiotics, maybe some anti-diarrhoea medicines, but not a lot. And they treated all those who resided in their catchment area, in their vicinity, including soldiers from the front lines, because that's who they were closest to. In the -- in these areas people resided throughout the war. The areas were never abandoned, if this is what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And another explanation regarding pain-killers. Were they class 3, of the morphine group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only the hospital had medicines from the group that you're referring to, two types. I remember two types. I don't know how they came to have them, where they came from or how, but I do know that in the hygienic institute they suddenly appeared. When I say suddenly, I mean suddenly. I was surprised to see when somebody unloaded this quantity, quite a large quantity of these strong pain-killers. One was Fortral and the other was morphine. I can't remember how much of what. I know that there was 3.000 units -- ampoules of one and 5.000 of another. And we used all that up much before the end of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Going back then to the hygiene institute and to the situation there, you just mentioned the equipment or the medicine that was used. Could you describe us a little bit further how the hospital was equipped to deal with all the patients that it received?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: Was we were dealing with the surgical hospital, then the equipment was surgical too, surgical equipment. Let me try and take this step-by-step. The operating table, one was sort of secondhand, if I can say it that way -- that way, and it had a very big drawback. That is to say you couldn't keep it level although there was hydraulic adjustment but it kept falling down and you had to keep raising it up and put something under it to keep it on that level. The other was an old tin table or bed which we used in a field hospital, but it was a collapsible one and you could use it. It was useful, although it didn't look very nice. Then at the beginning there was one operating lamp from pre-history, if I can put it that way. How it came to be there, I -- I don't know. It was a very old one. And we had the ventilation pumps to suck in the blood and various other bodily fluids that needed to be sucked out or in. We had anaesthesia equipment, two pieces of anaesthesia equipment. And as far as I know, they had formerly been owned by the JNA and had probably been brought in from one of the warehouses of South Camp or North Camp later on where the Yugoslav People's Army had their depots. They were ancient but the anaesthesias were glad with them because they did work. But we didn't have the essentials and when I mentioned anaesthetics although I'm not an expert in the field we were able to use barbiturates to have the patient fall asleep, and we managed keep the patient in a relaxed, as we call it, whereby the muscles are relaxed so that you can operate on the patient, because whenever you touch a nerve or muscle, even if the patient is asleep, the muscles react. So these were the two medicaments that we had. But what we didn't have is what is usual in an operating room. The oxygen tanks that you can see or if it's a centralised system then you don't see the tanks that we had to use. So we had to use ordinary air and use the equipment for anaesthesia, which rises and falls and enables the patient to breathe. This pump is called an ampoule [as interpreted] pump. It takes its name from the firm that produces it. There were no oxygen ampoules. Oxygen is a gas which is necessary to keep the patient in that sort of unconscious state, because the patient is unconscious. You relax your patient. You breathe instead of the patient, and all that's working is the patient's heart. So as far as I know, it was very difficult to maintain this unconscious state with what the anaesthesiologist had with the medical equipment they had and the level of anaesthesia was never high enough. Now, if I were to mention the instruments, well, we did have instruments. At the beginning I thought they were very good because I was a beginner, but I know better now. They were very primitive apparatuses which are no longer used, and we had to use them, and we didn't have enough of those either. We had to sterilise them all the time. We had to sterilise them in between surgical operations, and we didn't have complete sets of these either. There was always something lacking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, what about blood? Did you have any blood reserves. If your patients lost a lot of blood could you go ahead with transfusions? What did you do about that, about the blood situation, blood transfusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem was resolved in a very primitive way, the most primitive. When I say most primitive, in terms of medicine, medical science. There were bottles with fluids in order to determine the blood groups, and we had one set of that. We needed to conduct blood transfusions but how could you determine the blood group? So I and my colleague, Mrs. Focic, we went back to our university days and we remembered having picked each other, and I was 0 group, and we pricked each other as we did when we were at university. So we would test each of our blood groups and then test them with these samples and the test fluids that we had in our set and then constructed the chart that -- you can have a set chart ready-made, but we had to do this ourselves using the test board. But that's how we did it, so it's interesting. What you do now is, interaction between the donor blood and the recipient, but we had no way of doing that, of conducting tests like that, let alone any others. So the blood was administered later on. How shall I explain this to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, did you have enough blood or did you conduct in situ blood transfusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You've hit the nail on the head. I was just trying to say that and didn't manage to form a sentence. Yes, we provided blood on a need-to-have basis. We took it straight away and administered it straight away. We had nowhere to store it. We just had an ordinary fridge but not the proper fridge. So we never had any stockpiles of blood. You had to get the blood from a donor and give it to the patient straight away, on the spot; in situ, as you said.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Witness, going back to what you explained about the surgical influence and the need for them to be sterilised, what was the sterilisation equipment that you had at that time at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: I don't know whether I said at the beginning that there were two what we call autoclaves, a sterilisation unit like a big barrel under very high pressure, and wet sterilisation is conducted in this device so you need water and electricity. So at the beginning we used these two large sterilisation units, but when there was no more electricity then we couldn't do that any more. This equipment sterilisation equipment couldn't function any more. And then we moved to one autoclave or sterilisation unit which looked very funny to people who came in and saw it working. It was an old military sterilisation unit in which the temperature necessary for sterilisation was reached by using firewood. It had a funnel. So you would make a fire with the firewood, and it had to be behind the building on - what shall I call it? - a balcony, and that's where we sterilised with the bare necessities, what you had to sterilise with steam. And then there was dry sterilisation, which you needed for your instruments. We used a dry sterilising unit, very big with two large doors and with a lock that was faulty. So luckily it had two handles and we could hold the door closed by putting a pole to catch the two handles. This is something that we inherited, this sterilisation. It happened to be there in the service, and it was too big. I assume it's -- it stayed there because it was too big to carry anywhere else. So it just happened to be there, as luck would have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the sterilisation of instruments, did you have any patients die on you as a result of infection because the conditions were so poor and because the instruments weren't properly sterilised? Did you have cases where the operation had succeeded and you had managed to treat the wounds but unfortunately, given the bad conditions, the patient developed an infection, septicemia, and this led to their death ultimately? Because I assume that the medicines you had couldn't deal with septicemia. So were you able to deal with that kind of case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say that there were deaths resulting from unsatisfactory sterilisation, and here's why I say that. If there were wounds that had become inflamed, and there were that kind of wound, then my logical conclusion was to link that up, and I don't want to defend myself on the level of sterilisation, but I'd like to link it up to something we always say when it's a question of a war wound, and that is that it is primarily infected. The war wound is primarily inflicted. So that every inflammation when I do triage then I have to assume that the wound was caused by a dirty implement through dirty clothing that somebody died of septicemia, no, as far as I know that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: You also mentioned the lack of electricity and the water necessity. Could you explain to us what the situation was for these two necessary elements in the running of the hospital, water and electricity?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: Well, if you're asking me about that then in the first month, it was wonderful because everything worked. There was electricity and there was water too and we could as you all the equipment that we had properly. However, I don't know exactly when, I can't remember what date that was, but when we were left without electricity and water the situation became extremely difficult. You couldn't even wash your hands properly let alone anything else. With the water -- the water situation was as follows: There was a plastic reservoir, fairly large, I can't tell you exactly how large, but anyway it was there to hold water but it was also there to protect the window and there were sandbags piled up on top of it, and then there was another one, a little smaller, maybe half the size, and that one, that reservoir was in front of the kitchen window and you could see that on the photograph from that day where -- from that room where people spent the day. I don't know what to call it. And the third wasn't a reservoir; in fact, it was a receptacle which was not more than a hundred litres, could not take more man a hundred litres and it was under the -- in front of the window of the reception area. All those reservoirs were linked with a rubber tube where the tap was. Well, actually the tap didn't exist. We had to use a surgical clamp to shut the water off. That's the water situation. Now, the electricity situation is as follows: At the very beginning, even before the conflict began, as luck would have it, a man, I don't know who he was, he happened to pass by the building and met me, and he said, "Have you got a generator?" And I wondered, Why is he asking me whether we have a generator, and I said we didn't. And he said, "Well, there's a generator in a building -- in a house above us up on the hill. It's a building that contains some water pipes or something." And there was a generator there. And obviously he knew about this generator, which was a good quality generator and hadn't been used for too long. It was a test generator. And he suggested that we move it in. And I said, "All right. Fine." I don't know how we succeeded in doing this, but I think the very next day the generator was brought into the hospital. It was an enormous -- an enormous generator, very powerful. I can't express this in any numerical terms, but I know that a lot of other people latched on to the generator, the radio at one point, and some other administrative services of the War Presidencies or whatever else, some commands and so on, they latched onto that, and some private consumers, too, so that this caused some problems. But that wasn't the main problem. The main problem was that this generator used a lot of fuel and we couldn't get the fuel needed to operate it so that it wasn't working for long. The generator was only turned on when we had a major operation in the theatre. Otherwise, we worked in darkness or semi-darkness. What we used to light the hallway, and the hallway in the basement was the main area where we conducted triage and all the preparations, the examinations, and so on. So this hallway was lighted with two small car bulbs attached to a generator in the wall. So that's the water and electricity situation. And it would be better if you don't ask me about the sewage system. It was impossible to clean anything. We used -- there was one toilet that we all had to use and it was a terrible sight to behold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, at the beginning of this account you have said that the first month was fine. Could you just recall which month that was, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm speaking about the very beginning. It might have not have been one month. It might have been more or less, but if it's vital to you, well, I don't know the exact day that the power was cut. Let me try and remember. The 30th of June, for example. I know that there was electricity at the hygiene institute on the 30th of June. So that's more. That's a longer time than what I said. But after that I really can't remember that we had any lighting after that. That was the latest date when I know that I was in hospital and the light was as strong as it is here in the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Hvala.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: To go back to the operating room you said you didn't have a powerful lamp. After the electricity was cut down, what did you use to do the operations?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: When there was no more electricity, the lamp was linked to the generator if we had fuel to run the generator. If not, then we received from a doctor, I don't know which one but I know he was a doctor, from the Medicos del Mundo, Medicines of the World. We received three or four, no, I think it was three because I can remember that three of us had those lamps that you put on your forehead, on your head and forehead used by cave explorers. They were ordinary lamps, if I can say, made in China that are very cheap. They had a few batteries at the back and a few wires for this light in front. It wasn't one of those proper lamps with optic cables and the very high-tech ones. So when there was no electricity you would put this lamp on your head and I had one otherwise the person doing the operation would swap and have the lamp on his head.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: What about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Execution me. Dr. Rajkov, do you have any idea as to what the situation of hospital facilities on the other side of the Neretva was? Did you -- did you have any -- ever any contact, any exchange with colleagues from the -- from the -- I mean the political west of the Neretva, the HVO-controlled part of the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally did not have any direct contact with my colleagues on the west bank, as you say. However, following on logic, the pre-war hospital, which for some organisational or construction reasons were -- was located in some of these places, it existed -- this hospital existed before the war and it had all the necessary equipment that a hospital needs to have. So if we -- it was the surgical hospital. It existed before the war, during the war and after the war. So what it had then it had at that too. It wasn't under a siege. It wasn't under a blockade. If they needed something they could bring it in, install it, whatever. If you're asking me whether I have any notion of it, then that's my notion and I think I'm right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question that was asked a moment ago I wanted to ask myself, because in principle a doctor doesn't enter into political considerations and problems, but did it ever happen that -- did you ever try, regardless of the situation, to contact the other side for urgent emergency evacuations, for patients who demanded much more sophisticated treatment which needed better equipment and so on? Either with the people on the other side or the ICRC or anything like that? Or an UNPROFOR unit who -- which could use an armoured vehicle perhaps and transport patients. So did you look into any of these things at your level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At my level, that is to say me personally, no. I was the surgical labour force, if I can put it that way. I was not in any management position or position of leadership. I know that our head of hospital did have contacts with what we call the Spanish Battalion. I don't know if that's the proper name, but probably through them with someone on the other side perhaps or some international organisation. I know that evacuations were organised, and I know on two occasions they were unsuccessful. After I personally wrote out a list very, very quickly because they were moving out, and it was the Spanish Battalion's armoured vehicles, I made out a list of patients to be evacuated and one or two hours later here they were back again. What happened? They didn't let them pass. That's all I know. Who didn't let them pass? Probably not the Bosnian side. I don't know. Anyway, that was the answer: They didn't let us pass. As to another case I know that the patient or patients were supposed to be evacuated by helicopter and then that helicopter was blocked in Medjugorje think it was. I personally do have one example of an evacuation but from a later period and it went via SpaBat and via the liaison officer. We needed 24 hours to evacuate it. But that was a long time later. Maybe it was even after the conflict had stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Except for the usual staff at the hospital, were there during the period after 9 May medical staff coming from the hospital to help, coming from out of East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: Whether after the 9th of May there was still medical staff that came to help us? Ah. Well, yes. Yes, they did, because they offered their services. Anybody with any medical knowledge who had perhaps worked within a hospital and lived on the eastern side did, but that wasn't -- it didn't improve matters, and there were a few -- although there were a few elderly and experienced nurses, but very few of them had worked in surgery, had worked in an operating theatre. But we didn't have any doctor coming in, no. The number of the staff was constant. What we had at the beginning we had later on, the same number of doctors and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: What about doctors coming from outside East Mostar, for instance, from West Mostar, after the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: From West Mostar. Nobody ever came to our hospital from West Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Were there doctors or nurses from any other organisations or hospitals that would come at one point and help you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, and I say first and foremost because they were the first and were the most numerous, were doctors from the Medicos del Mundo organisation, and most of them were Spaniards, were Spanish, although there was an elderly British doctor and I think a few others from other countries. But I remember this one in particular. Then there was some medical staff. I say medical staff intentionally because, as far as I remember from the Medecins Sans Frontieres, members of the services such as epidemiology, hygiene, some kind of child care and protection, not paediatrics, but they would come, and there were a few doctors coming in sporadically in waves from time to time, teams from Sarajevo. That was it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We're going to have to adjourn for the day, but one more question from me as a point of clarification. You've answered a lot of questions. This will facilitate everyone's task tomorrow. Did it ever happen that you administered care and attention to Croats who might have been wounded, who were prisoners who happened to be there in the East Mostar zone? Did you ever do that, that is to say care for Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not that it happened. It was customary. It was very usual. We gave surgical help and anything else to everybody. Not only prisoners from the HVO but, for example, I remember a soldier from the Spanish Battalion who was hit by the bridge, and we have him in our protocol logbook. We took them all in, treated them in hospital, operated on them. I myself operated on a number of them, I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. We have to adjourn for the day. We have four hours left tomorrow. A lot of questions have been tackled. I hope that the Prosecution will focus so that the Defence can go ahead and perhaps there's some medical specialists among the Defence teams. Doctor, I wish you a pleasant evening. On behalf of myself and my colleagues. As you are a witness of justice, please do not contact any of the parties. And we shall reconvene tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: reconvened on Thursday, the 25th day of January, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
